lessons.title: Prompts and Conversation Context · Level 2
lessons.slo: Distinguish prompt types and explain how a model continues a conversation.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the definition.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The definition would blur a request with general guidance.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the prompt type, then state that it asks for a specific response or instruction.

exercises.correct_answer: A user prompt asks for a specific response or instruction
exercises.explanation: A user prompt requests a particular response or instruction, unlike broad system guidance.

exercises.question_text: Earlier prompts and responses can be included later as ___.

parts.text: Earlier prompts and responses can be included later as

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The term would name something other than prior chat context.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use "conversation history" for earlier prompts and responses.

exercises.explanation: Conversation history carries earlier discussion into later prompts.

exercises.question_text: An executive needs a summary of generative-AI adoption. Which details belong in the user prompt to make that request specific? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask for no more than six bullets
options.rationale: This specifies the required output structure. It makes the requested result more precise.
Naming the audience adds useful context. It helps shape the requested summary.

options.text: Set the app's permanent tone rule
options.rationale: A permanent rule is broad behavior guidance, not a detail of one summary request. It belongs in a system prompt.
options.better_fit: It fits a system prompt.

feedback.intrinsic: The immediate request becomes mixed with a future rule.
feedback.instructional: Use user prompts for the specific task and system prompts for persistent behavior.

options.rationale: Prior context is useful only when needed to interpret a follow-up. It is not required to define this new summary request.
options.better_fit: It fits conversation history for a context-dependent follow-up.

feedback.intrinsic: The request may become crowded with irrelevant messages.
feedback.instructional: Specify audience and format; include history only when context is necessary.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Audience and format make the user request specific.

exercises.question_text: An executive first discusses adopting generative AI, then asks, "What are common privacy-related risks?" What should the app include so the assistant understands the topic?

options.rationale: A summary of earlier prompts and responses supplies the topic for the follow-up. It connects privacy risks to generative-AI adoption.
The new question does not name what the privacy risks concern. It needs the earlier topic for proper interpretation.
options.better_fit: It fits a question that states its topic explicitly.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant may answer about privacy generally.
feedback.instructional: Include conversation history when a follow-up depends on an earlier topic.

options.rationale: A tone rule changes how the response sounds. It does not identify the prior topic.
options.better_fit: It fits setting response behavior.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may have the right style but miss the context.
feedback.instructional: Use conversation history to preserve the earlier topic.

options.rationale: A predicted token is generated during a completion. It is not a record of prior conversation.
options.better_fit: It fits next-token prediction.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant still lacks the earlier discussion.
feedback.instructional: Earlier prompts and responses provide context; predicted tokens are generated afterward.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Summarized earlier messages provide the needed context.

exercises.question_text: The decoder repeatedly selects the most probable next ___ in a sequence.

parts.text: The decoder repeatedly selects the most probable next
in a sequence.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The missing term would not name the item added to the sequence.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A token is the unit predicted next.

exercises.explanation: A decoder builds a completion by predicting one token at a time.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the masked-attention training steps.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The model would compare or adjust before making a fair prediction.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Hide later tokens, predict, compare with the known token, then adjust weights.

exercises.correct_answer: Ignore later tokens Predict next token Compare known token Adjust learned weights
exercises.explanation: Future tokens are hidden before prediction; the known next token is then used to measure error and adjust weights.

exercises.question_text: A writer asks an AI assistant to continue "When my dog was a ...". Which next token should the assistant choose?

options.rationale: "Puppy" naturally continues a phrase about a dog when it was young. It is more probable in this context than the alternatives.
A cat is an animal, but it does not naturally describe the dog in this phrase. It is less probable given the preceding words.
options.better_fit: It could fit a sentence about a different animal.

feedback.intrinsic: The sentence shifts away from the dog's earlier life.
feedback.instructional: Choose the token most supported by the preceding sequence.

options.rationale: This word does not fit the meaning established by the phrase. It is much less probable than a word about a young dog.
options.better_fit: It could fit a sentence about an object or activity.

feedback.intrinsic: The continuation becomes unrelated to the dog.
feedback.instructional: Next-token prediction favors continuations that fit context.

options.rationale: A system prompt is broad response guidance, not a token completing this sentence. It cannot serve as the likely continuation here.
options.better_fit: It would fit an application's behavior rule.

feedback.intrinsic: The writer receives guidance instead of a completion.
feedback.instructional: The model must choose a token that continues the sequence.

exercises.explanation: Correct. "Puppy" is the most likely continuation.

exercises.question_text: A team trains a decoder on complete sentences. Which actions let it learn to predict the next token without leaking future words? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hide tokens after the current position
options.rationale: This prevents future words from influencing the current prediction. It is the masking step used in decoder training.

options.text: Compare the prediction with the known next token
options.rationale: The complete training sequence supplies the known target token. Comparing prediction and target supports error reduction.

options.text: Use later tokens to make the prediction
options.rationale: Later tokens must be hidden for the current prediction. Using them leaks future information.
options.better_fit: It would fit a task that is not causal next-token prediction.

feedback.intrinsic: The model gets an unfair hint from the future.
feedback.instructional: Masked attention requires predictions to use earlier tokens only.

options.rationale: A style rule affects response tone, not how training hides future tokens. It does not address prediction leakage.
options.better_fit: This would fit a system prompt.

feedback.intrinsic: The team sets style but does not prevent leakage.
feedback.instructional: Use masking for training mechanics and a system prompt for tone.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Mask future tokens and compare predictions with known targets.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the prompt-design steps.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The request may lack a clear task or response shape.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: State the task first, then add context, an example, and a format.

exercises.correct_answer: State the task Add useful context Give an example Request a format
exercises.explanation: A strong prompt first makes the task clear, then adds context, an example, and desired structure.

exercises.question_text: A ___ can require a model to respond in a friendly tone.

parts.text: A
can require a model to respond in a friendly tone.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The term would not name the source of ongoing tone guidance.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use "system prompt" for behavior, tone, and constraints.

exercises.explanation: Friendly tone is broad guidance, so it belongs in a system prompt.

exercises.question_text: A manager needs an executive summary of generative-AI adoption, but the first result is too broad. Which changes should the manager make? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Naming the audience adds context that shapes the summary. It makes the request more specific.
Requesting a format clarifies how the result should be structured. It makes the output more usable.
This request omits the specific topic, audience, and format. It is unlikely to produce a focused executive summary.
options.better_fit: It fits a broad casual conversation starter.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may receive a general answer unrelated to the briefing.
feedback.instructional: Specify the topic, audience, and desired structure.

options.rationale: Removing a format makes the desired output less clear. Structure requests often make a response easier to use.
options.better_fit: It fits a situation with no required response structure.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may be difficult to use in the briefing.
feedback.instructional: Keep the requested structure to clarify the goal.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Audience and format make the prompt more focused.

exercises.question_text: A company builds an expenses assistant that must respond cheerfully to every employee. Where should the application place this ongoing rule?

options.rationale: An ongoing rule about response style is broad behavior guidance. A system prompt is designed for this purpose.
A user prompt asks for a particular response. It is not the usual place for a rule applying to every employee.
options.better_fit: It fits an employee's specific expense question.

feedback.intrinsic: The tone rule is not established globally.
feedback.instructional: Put persistent behavior rules in the system prompt.

options.rationale: Conversation history stores prior exchanges. It does not establish a permanent tone requirement.
options.better_fit: It fits a follow-up about an earlier expense discussion.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant may remember an exchange but lacks the style rule.
feedback.instructional: History supplies context; a system prompt supplies behavior guidance.

options.rationale: Retrieved policy text can ground an expense answer. It does not control how every answer should sound.
options.better_fit: It fits answering a policy-specific expense question.

feedback.intrinsic: The answer may be accurate but not consistently cheerful.
feedback.instructional: Retrieved text adds facts; a system prompt sets the style rule.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A system prompt carries ongoing style guidance.

lessons.title: Prompts and Conversation Context · Level 3
lessons.slo: Distinguish prompt types and explain how a model continues a conversation.

exercises.question_text: What is prompt engineering?

options.rationale: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing prompts to improve responses. Both the model and the prompt affect quality.
Retrieval augmented generation adds retrieved information to a prompt. It is not the general practice of designing prompts.
options.better_fit: It fits RAG.

options.rationale: Behavior rules are set with a system prompt. Prompt engineering improves prompt wording and structure.
options.better_fit: It fits a system prompt.

options.rationale: Next-token prediction is how a decoder generates a completion. It is not how a person designs a prompt.
options.better_fit: It fits next-token prediction.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Prompt engineering designs prompts for better results.

exercises.question_text: Which can be set by a system prompt? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Tone is part of the broad guidance a system prompt can establish. It can apply across responses.

options.text: A rule the model must follow
options.rationale: Constraints are rules for model behavior. A system prompt can set them.

options.text: A specific request for a summary
options.rationale: A summary request asks for one particular response. That is a user-prompt function.
options.better_fit: It fits a user prompt.

options.rationale: Earlier messages are conversation history. They provide context, not behavior rules.
options.better_fit: It fits conversation history.

exercises.explanation: Correct. System prompts can set tone and constraints.

exercises.question_text: Response quality depends on both the language model and the prompts submitted to it.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A vague prompt may still yield an unhelpful result.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Response quality depends on both the model and the submitted prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Better prompt design can improve a capable model's results.

exercises.question_text: A system prompt is normally the human user's specific question for the model.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Broad rules and one-time requests would be confused.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: System prompts set behavior; user prompts ask for specific responses.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A specific human question is a user prompt.

exercises.question_text: What gives a follow-up question context from an earlier chat?

options.rationale: Conversation history includes earlier prompts and responses with later prompts. It gives follow-up questions ongoing context.
A system prompt sets behavior, tone, and constraints. It does not carry prior-chat details.
options.better_fit: It fits overall behavior guidance.

options.rationale: A user prompt is the new question or instruction. It does not itself preserve prior discussion.
options.better_fit: It fits asking the follow-up question.

options.rationale: Masked attention is a decoder-training technique. It does not preserve chat messages.
options.better_fit: It fits decoder training.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Conversation history provides prior context.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe masked attention? Select all that apply.

options.text: It ignores tokens after the current token
options.rationale: Masked attention hides tokens after the current position. This keeps predictions based on earlier tokens.

options.text: It is used while training the decoder
options.rationale: Masked attention is used during decoder training on complete sequences. The known next token can then be used for comparison.

options.text: It sets response tone and constraints
options.rationale: Tone and constraints are response guidance. Masked attention is a decoder-training technique.
options.better_fit: This describes a system prompt.

options.rationale: Retrieval adds information to a prompt. Masked attention hides future tokens during training.
options.better_fit: This describes retrieval augmented generation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Masked attention hides later tokens during decoder training.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the conversation-context process.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The follow-up may be answered without its needed topic.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: First discuss a topic, then ask a follow-up and include the earlier context.

exercises.correct_answer: Discuss a topic Ask a follow-up Include earlier context Answer stays relevant
exercises.explanation: An earlier discussion gives a follow-up its context when that context is included.

exercises.question_text: After comparing a prediction with the known next token, training adjusts the model's ___ to reduce error over later iterations.

parts.text: After comparing a prediction with the known next token, training adjusts the model's
to reduce error over later iterations.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The sentence would not identify what training changes to improve future predictions.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Training updates learned weights after measuring prediction error.

exercises.explanation: Masked-attention training compares predictions with known targets and adjusts learned weights to reduce error.

exercises.question_text: The decoder repeatedly selects the most probable next ___ in a sequence.

parts.text: The decoder repeatedly selects the most probable next
in a sequence.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The missing term would not name the item added to the sequence.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A token is the unit predicted next.

exercises.explanation: A decoder builds a completion by predicting one token at a time.

exercises.question_text: What is a user prompt?

options.rationale: A user prompt asks for a response to a particular question or instruction. It is input to the model.

options.text: Overall behavior set by an app
options.rationale: Overall behavior is broad guidance. A user prompt instead asks for a particular response.
options.better_fit: It fits a system prompt.

options.rationale: A record of earlier messages is conversation history. It provides context for later prompts.
options.better_fit: It fits conversation history.

options.rationale: A predicted token is generated in a completion. A user prompt is model input.
options.better_fit: It fits next-token prediction.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A user prompt is a specific request.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the steps of next-token prediction.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The next prediction would lack the newly generated context.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Predict, add the token, then use the expanded sequence until an end is predicted.

exercises.correct_answer: Predict a token Add it to sequence Use expanded sequence Stop at sequence end
exercises.explanation: The predicted token is added to the sequence, which becomes context for the next prediction.

exercises.question_text: A person or an application can create a user prompt.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Valid application-created requests would be overlooked.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: User prompts may be created by a person or by an application.

exercises.explanation: Correct. An application can generate a user prompt on a person's behalf.

lessons.title: Grounded and Well-Designed Responses · Level 1
lessons.slo: Choose prompt and retrieval practices that produce a more relevant response.

exercises.question_text: Which prompt is clear and specific?

options.text: Summarize travel risks for managers in four bullets
options.rationale: This request states a task, a topic, an audience, and a format. Those details make the instruction clear and specific.
This request does not state what should be done with the topic. It also gives no audience or desired format.
options.better_fit: This fits a broad opening question when no particular outcome is needed. Add instructions and context when a useful work response is required.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may cover an unhelpful part of travel or use the wrong level of detail.
feedback.instructional: State the task clearly, then add useful context such as the audience and desired format.

options.rationale: A sample can show a desired style. This request does not state what content should be written.
options.better_fit: This fits style guidance when paired with a complete content request. Use it when the desired style needs to be made concrete.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may copy a tone without addressing the travel task the person needs.
feedback.instructional: Examples help with style, but a clear prompt also states the topic and the requested work.

options.error_type: Confuses full instructions with structure alone
options.rationale: A table is a structure requirement. By itself, it does not say what information belongs in the table.
options.better_fit: This fits a format instruction added to a complete prompt. Use it when the content and audience are already clear.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may be organized as a table but have no clear subject to cover.
feedback.instructional: Structure is helpful, but it needs a clear task and topic around it.

exercises.explanation: Correct—this prompt specifies the task, topic, audience, and format. Those details support a more useful response.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe a grounded response? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A grounded response is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt. That information gives the response a basis for answering.

options.text: It can answer from retrieved policy text
options.rationale: Retrieved policy text can be supplied in the prompt. A response based on that relevant text is grounded.

options.text: It must use only chat history
options.rationale: Conversation history can provide context from earlier messages. Grounding is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt and is not limited to chat history.
options.better_fit: This fits preserving prior conversation context. It is useful when a follow-up question depends on an earlier exchange.

feedback.intrinsic: A reply may miss the relevant policy facts if earlier messages are the only source used.
feedback.instructional: Grounding is about relevant supplied information, not about using only prior chat messages.

options.text: It must be a numbered list
options.rationale: A numbered list is a way to organize a reply. Format alone does not determine whether a response is grounded.
options.better_fit: This fits a request for response structure. Use it when the answer should be organized in numbered steps.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may be easy to scan but still not be based on relevant information.
feedback.instructional: A grounded response needs relevant supplied facts. A numbered list only controls organization.

exercises.explanation: Correct—grounded responses use relevant information supplied in the prompt. Retrieved policy text is one way to provide that information.

exercises.question_text: Adding the topic, audience, and desired format can make a prompt more useful.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Without these details, a response may be relevant in general but unsuitable for the intended reader.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: When they matter, name the topic, audience, and desired format so the request is clear and specific.

exercises.explanation: Correct—topic, audience, and format add useful context. They help make the requested response clearer.

exercises.question_text: A response is grounded when it is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Without relevant supplied information, a company-policy answer may stay generic.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Grounding means basing the response on relevant information included in the prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct—relevant information supplied in the prompt gives the response its grounding. This can make an answer more relevant to the question.

exercises.question_text: What does retrieval augmented generation (RAG) do?

options.text: Adds retrieved information to a prompt
options.rationale: RAG retrieves relevant information, such as documents or emails. It adds that information to the prompt with the user's question.
Earlier messages can provide conversation context. RAG instead retrieves relevant information and adds it to the prompt.
options.better_fit: This fits conversation history. It is useful when a later question needs context from an earlier exchange.

feedback.intrinsic: The answer could miss important company information and stay generic.
feedback.instructional: Keep the two ideas separate: conversation history uses earlier messages, while RAG retrieves relevant information.

options.rationale: Behavior and tone are set through a system prompt. RAG supplies relevant information for the response to use.
options.better_fit: This fits a system prompt. It is used to define behavior, tone, and constraints.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply might sound right but still lack the facts needed for the question.
feedback.instructional: Style guidance affects how a reply is written; RAG adds relevant information to what the reply can use.

options.rationale: A list or table tells how to organize a reply. It does not retrieve information to add to the prompt.
options.better_fit: This fits a response-structure request. Use it when the reply should be organized as bullets, a table, or a numbered list.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may be neatly organized but still not be based on the needed facts.
feedback.instructional: Structure changes organization. RAG retrieves relevant information so the response can be grounded.

exercises.explanation: Correct—RAG retrieves relevant information and adds it to the prompt. That added context supports a more relevant response.

exercises.question_text: When is an example useful in a prompt? Select all that apply.

options.text: When a desired style needs clarity
options.rationale: An example makes a desired style concrete. It helps show what the writer means by that style.

options.text: When you want the model to copy a style
options.rationale: Examples help a model reproduce a requested style. They provide a concrete pattern for the writing.

options.text: When you need retrieved policy facts
options.rationale: Policy facts are relevant information that should be retrieved and added to the prompt. A style example does not retrieve or provide those facts.
options.better_fit: This fits retrieval augmented generation. Use it when a response needs relevant documents or other information.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may match a style but fail to state the policy facts needed for the decision.
feedback.instructional: Use an example to show style. Retrieve relevant policy information when the response needs factual grounding.

options.text: When you need prior chat context
options.rationale: Prior chat context comes from earlier prompts and responses. A style example is added to show the desired writing style.
options.better_fit: This fits conversation history. It is useful when a follow-up question depends on an earlier exchange.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may lose the earlier discussion if a style sample is used as though it were chat history.
feedback.instructional: Examples guide style; conversation history preserves prior context. Choose the one that matches the need.

exercises.explanation: Correct—examples are useful when a desired style needs to be shown clearly. They help the response reproduce that style.

exercises.question_text: RAG uses only earlier conversation messages to add information to a prompt.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Using only earlier messages can leave a policy question without the policy details it needs.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Conversation history and RAG both add context, but they get it differently: RAG retrieves relevant information and adds it to the prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct—earlier messages are conversation history. RAG retrieves relevant information such as documents or emails.

exercises.question_text: Which request specifies a response structure?

options.rationale: A numbered list tells how the response should be organized. It is a direct structure requirement.
This states a topic and task. It does not say whether the response should use bullets, a table, or another organization.
options.better_fit: This fits a content request when no particular format is needed. Add a structure instruction when organization matters.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may explain the topic but be harder for the reader to scan than needed.
feedback.instructional: To specify structure, state how the response should be organized, such as in bullets, a table, or a numbered list.

options.text: Use this response as a style sample
options.rationale: A style sample guides the tone or writing style. It does not specify how the reply should be organized.
options.better_fit: This fits making a desired style concrete. Use it when the response should resemble a particular writing style.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may match a tone but still lack the requested organization.
feedback.instructional: A sample affects style. A numbered list, table, or bullet points affect response structure.

options.rationale: Retrieving the expense policy adds relevant information to a prompt. It does not state the response's organization.
options.better_fit: This fits grounding an expense-policy answer in relevant policy information. It can be combined with a format request.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may have the right policy facts but be organized in an unhelpful way.
feedback.instructional: Retrieval provides information; response structure tells how to present that information.

exercises.explanation: Correct—a numbered list tells how the response should be organized. That is a request for response structure.

exercises.question_text: Providing an example is mainly a way to retrieve policy documents for a prompt.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A policy answer may lack the needed rules if a style sample is used instead of retrieving relevant policy information.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Keep the purposes distinct: examples show style, while RAG retrieves relevant information such as documents.

exercises.explanation: Correct—retrieving relevant documents is RAG. An example is used to make a requested style concrete.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The relationship between supplied information and response relevance becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Connect the cause to the outcome: relevant prompt information can make a response more relevant.

exercises.correct_answer: Relevant prompt information can make a response more relevant
exercises.explanation: Relevant information supplied with a request gives a response a factual basis and can make it more relevant. This differs from merely preserving earlier conversation context.

exercises.question_text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more ___ than vague prompts.

parts.text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more
than vague prompts.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A vague request can lead to a response that does not match the intended task.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The missing phrase is clear and specific. Examples show style, and response structure organizes a reply, but explicit instructions make the prompt itself clear.

exercises.explanation: Explicit instructions make the requested task easier to understand than vague language. Examples and response structure can help too, but they are particular additions rather than the overall quality named here.

exercises.question_text: Asking for bullet points, a table, or a numbered list can improve response organization.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A useful answer may be harder to scan if its organization is left unspecified.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Ask for bullet points, a table, or a numbered list when a particular organization will help the reader.

exercises.explanation: Correct—bullet points, tables, and numbered lists are structure requirements. They guide how the response is organized.

flashcards.back: RAG retrieves relevant information and adds it to a prompt.
A response based on relevant information supplied in its prompt.
Examples help the model reproduce a requested style.
The requested organization, such as bullets, tables, or numbered lists.

lessons.title: Grounded and Well-Designed Responses · Level 2
lessons.slo: Choose prompt and retrieval practices that produce a more relevant response.

exercises.question_text: Providing an example can help a model reproduce a requested style.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Without a concrete style guide, the reply may not match the approved tone a writer needs.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Provide an example when you want a particular style and need to show what that style looks like.

exercises.explanation: Correct—an example makes the desired style concrete. It helps guide the wording and tone of the response.

exercises.question_text: A response is grounded when it is based only on the conversation history.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Relying only on earlier messages may leave out the facts needed for the current question.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Earlier conversation can be useful context. A grounded response is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct—conversation history can add context, but it is not the definition of grounding. Grounding uses relevant information supplied in the prompt.

exercises.question_text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more ___ than vague prompts.

parts.text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more
than vague prompts.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A vague request can lead to a response that does not match the intended task.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The missing phrase is clear and specific. Examples show style, and response structure organizes a reply, but explicit instructions make the prompt itself clear.

exercises.explanation: Explicit instructions make the requested task easier to understand than vague language. Examples and response structure can help too, but they are particular additions rather than the overall quality named here.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The purpose of the sample becomes unclear when its connection to the desired style is broken.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Keep the logic together: provide a sample when the desired style needs to be made concrete.

exercises.correct_answer: Provide an example when the desired style needs to be made concrete
exercises.explanation: A style can be hard to describe with general words alone. Providing a concrete sample helps show the style the response should reproduce.

exercises.question_text: A communications employee must ask an assistant for a summary of generative AI adoption for corporate executives. Which prompt should the employee send?

options.text: Summarize AI adoption for executives in six bullets
options.rationale: This request identifies the topic, audience, and desired format. It gives explicit instructions for the needed summary.
The task and topic are present, but the audience is missing. The requested format is also not stated.
options.better_fit: This fits a situation where any audience and format are acceptable. Add more context for a corporate-executive summary.

feedback.intrinsic: The employee may receive a summary that is not suited to executives or is hard to scan.
feedback.instructional: Add the intended audience and format when they matter. Here, executives and six bullets make the request more useful.

options.rationale: A writing sample can guide style. This instruction does not ask for a summary or identify the topic and audience.
options.better_fit: This fits style guidance alongside a complete request. Use it when a desired style needs to be shown.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may imitate a style but fail to summarize generative AI adoption for executives.
feedback.instructional: A complete prompt says what to do and for whom. Add a sample only when style guidance is also needed.

options.error_type: Confuses complete prompt with structure alone
options.rationale: This requests an organization but gives no topic or audience. It is only one part of a clear and specific prompt.
options.better_fit: This fits a format instruction added to a full request. Use it when the content and audience have already been stated.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may be numbered but not address the executive summary task.
feedback.instructional: A structure request helps organize a response; it does not replace the topic, task, and audience.

exercises.explanation: Correct—it clearly names the topic, audience, and format. That gives the assistant a focused request to follow.

exercises.question_text: A customer-support writer needs an assistant to create replies in the same style as an approved customer reply. Which actions should the writer take? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: The approved reply provides a concrete model of the desired style. Including it gives the writer's style request something specific to follow.

options.text: Ask the model to follow its style
options.rationale: This instruction explains how the approved reply should be used. It connects the sample to the new replies being requested.
Expense-policy sections provide factual context for expense questions. They do not demonstrate the style of an approved customer reply.
options.better_fit: This fits a reply that must answer an expense-policy question. Use it when relevant policy facts are needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The new reply may include unrelated expense details and still fail to match the approved customer style.
feedback.instructional: For style matching, provide the approved reply and ask to follow its style. Retrieve policy sections only when policy facts are needed.

options.rationale: Earlier messages can maintain conversational context. They do not necessarily show the approved style the writer wants to reproduce.
options.better_fit: This fits retaining context from an ongoing exchange. It is useful when a follow-up depends on what was previously said.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may continue the conversation but not match the approved customer-reply style.
feedback.instructional: Conversation history preserves context. A selected approved reply is the concrete style example needed here.

exercises.explanation: Correct—include the approved reply and explicitly ask to follow its style. Together, those actions make the desired style concrete.

exercises.question_text: The approach that retrieves relevant documents and adds them to a prompt is ___.

parts.text: The approach that retrieves relevant documents and adds them to a prompt is

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The prompt would not name the approach used to bring relevant documents into the answer.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. Do not confuse it with conversation history or with the grounded response that relevant information can support.

exercises.explanation: The term names a process that first retrieves relevant information and then augments the prompt with it. Conversation history uses earlier messages, while a grounded response is the result of using relevant supplied information.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The relationship between supplied information and response relevance becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Connect the cause to the outcome: relevant prompt information can make a response more relevant.

exercises.correct_answer: Relevant prompt information can make a response more relevant
exercises.explanation: Relevant information supplied with a request gives a response a factual basis and can make it more relevant. This differs from merely preserving earlier conversation context.

exercises.question_text: An employee asks an expenses assistant for the maximum travel claim. Before the assistant answers, what should its developer have the app do?

options.rationale: The relevant policy sections contain the organization-specific information needed for the question. They can be added to the prompt before a response is generated.

options.text: Use only the employee's last message
options.rationale: The employee's question identifies the topic but does not provide the maximum claim amount. Relevant policy information is still needed.
options.better_fit: This fits using the latest request as part of conversation context. It is not enough when the answer depends on company policy.

feedback.intrinsic: The employee may receive a generic answer instead of the company rule.
feedback.instructional: The question tells what to look for. Retrieve the relevant travel-policy sections to provide the facts.

options.rationale: A numbered list can make a response easier to read. It does not provide the travel-expense rule.
options.better_fit: This fits a request to organize an answer. It can be added after the relevant policy is supplied.

feedback.intrinsic: The employee may get a tidy list without learning the correct claim limit.
feedback.instructional: Format and factual grounding solve different needs. Retrieve the policy when the question depends on policy facts.

options.error_type: Confuses retrieval with examples in prompts
options.rationale: A style sample can show how a reply should sound. It does not supply the travel-expense policy.
options.better_fit: This fits a request to match a desired writing style. Use it when tone or style needs to be made concrete.

feedback.intrinsic: The answer could sound polished while still missing the correct company rule.
feedback.instructional: A style example guides wording. Relevant retrieved policy information supplies the facts for this question.

exercises.explanation: Correct—retrieving the relevant travel-expense policy is the RAG step. It gives the prompt information that can ground the answer.

exercises.question_text: A request for bullet points or a table specifies the response ___.

parts.text: A request for bullet points or a table specifies the response

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The requested reply could be organized in the wrong way because the organization term is missing.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The missing term is structure. Examples in prompts guide style, while clear and specific prompts describe the quality of the overall request.

exercises.explanation: Bullet points and tables determine how a response is organized. They do not themselves show a writing style or describe the overall clarity of the prompt.

exercises.question_text: A manager asks an expenses assistant about travel claims. The assistant must answer using the company rules. Which actions help make its answer grounded? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Relevant travel-policy sections provide the company rules for the answer. Supplying them in the prompt grounds the response.
The manager's question identifies what information the response should address. Combined with relevant policy sections, it helps focus the grounded answer.

options.text: Use a generic answer without policy text
options.rationale: A generic answer is not based on the company's supplied travel rules. It may not answer the manager's policy question with relevant information.
options.better_fit: This fits a situation with no organization-specific information available. It is weaker when company rules are required.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may receive advice that does not match the company's travel rules.
feedback.instructional: For a grounded policy answer, include relevant policy information with the manager's question.

options.rationale: A table tells how to organize information. It does not provide the company rules on which an answer must be based.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to compare or organize information in a table. It can be used together with relevant supplied policy sections.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may get a clear table that still lacks the company rule.
feedback.instructional: Structure can improve readability, but grounding requires relevant information in the prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct—include the question and the relevant travel-policy sections. The policy sections provide the facts that ground the response.

exercises.question_text: A manager asks an assistant to prepare project risks for a meeting. The manager needs the risks presented clearly. Which instruction should be added?

options.text: Present the risks in a table
options.rationale: A table specifies how the project risks should be organized. It can help present the risks clearly for the meeting.
A friendly sample reply guides tone or style. It does not specify how to organize project risks.
options.better_fit: This fits a situation where a friendly writing style is needed. It is useful when the desired tone needs a concrete sample.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may receive a friendly-sounding response that is still difficult to scan in the meeting.
feedback.instructional: Use a table when the need is clear organization. Use a sample reply when the need is to demonstrate tone or style.

options.rationale: Travel-policy sections provide information for travel-expense questions. They do not organize project risks for a meeting.
options.better_fit: This fits a travel-expense question that needs relevant company policy information. It does not address this formatting need.

feedback.intrinsic: The meeting material could include unrelated travel information and still present risks poorly.
feedback.instructional: Retrieved information adds facts. A table is the instruction that directly controls how the project risks are presented.

options.rationale: The project-risk topic is already part of the request. This instruction does not say how the risks should be organized.
options.better_fit: This fits adding topic context to an incomplete request. It is unnecessary when the topic is already clear.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may still get an unstructured list that is difficult to use during the meeting.
feedback.instructional: The missing need is organization. Add a format instruction such as presenting the risks in a table.

exercises.explanation: Correct—a table is a clear response-structure request. It tells how to present the project risks for easier scanning.

lessons.title: Grounded and Well-Designed Responses · Level 3
lessons.slo: Choose prompt and retrieval practices that produce a more relevant response.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe a grounded response? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A grounded response is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt. That information gives the response a basis for answering.

options.text: It can answer from retrieved policy text
options.rationale: Retrieved policy text can be supplied in the prompt. A response based on that relevant text is grounded.

options.text: It must use only chat history
options.rationale: Conversation history can provide context from earlier messages. Grounding is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt and is not limited to chat history.
options.better_fit: This fits preserving prior conversation context. It is useful when a follow-up question depends on an earlier exchange.

feedback.intrinsic: A reply may miss the relevant policy facts if earlier messages are the only source used.
feedback.instructional: Grounding is about relevant supplied information, not about using only prior chat messages.

options.text: It must be a numbered list
options.rationale: A numbered list is a way to organize a reply. Format alone does not determine whether a response is grounded.
options.better_fit: This fits a request for response structure. Use it when the answer should be organized in numbered steps.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may be easy to scan but still not be based on relevant information.
feedback.instructional: A grounded response needs relevant supplied facts. A numbered list only controls organization.

exercises.explanation: Correct—grounded responses use relevant information supplied in the prompt. Retrieved policy text is one way to provide that information.

exercises.question_text: Providing an example can help a model reproduce a requested style.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Without a concrete style guide, the reply may not match the approved tone a writer needs.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Provide an example when you want a particular style and need to show what that style looks like.

exercises.explanation: Correct—an example makes the desired style concrete. It helps guide the wording and tone of the response.

exercises.question_text: Clear, specific prompts work better because they avoid stating explicit instructions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Avoiding instructions can leave the response focused on the wrong task.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Clear prompts work better because they explicitly say what is needed, rather than leaving the request vague.

exercises.explanation: Correct—clear, specific prompts state explicit instructions or questions. Vague language gives less direction.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The reason for asking for a format becomes unclear when the action and its result are out of sequence.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Put the action first, then its purpose: ask for structure to improve how the response is organized.

exercises.correct_answer: Ask for structure to improve how the model organizes its response
exercises.explanation: A structure requirement affects the organization of the reply, not the information it contains. Asking for bullets, a table, or numbered steps can make the organization clearer.

exercises.question_text: A developer sees that an expense assistant’s answers do not match the company’s travel rules. Which choices best support answers that match those rules? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Relevant expense-policy information supplies the rules the answer needs. A response based on it can be grounded in those rules.
Retrieval finds the information most relevant to the travel question. Those sections can then be provided in the prompt.

options.text: Rely only on previous chat messages
options.rationale: Earlier chat messages may preserve context but may not include the travel rules. They do not guarantee that the response is based on relevant policy information.
options.better_fit: This fits a follow-up that needs earlier conversational context. It does not replace supplying the needed policy facts.

feedback.intrinsic: The answers may continue to disagree with the rules if the rules are not in the earlier chat.
feedback.instructional: Use earlier messages for continuity when helpful, but provide relevant travel-policy information to ground rule-based answers.

options.rationale: A style sample shows how a response should sound. It does not state the company travel rules.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to make a desired tone or writing style concrete. It can accompany factual policy information but cannot replace it.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may sound appropriate while still giving the wrong policy guidance.
feedback.instructional: Use a style sample for style. Use relevant supplied policy information when the response must match company rules.

exercises.explanation: Correct—retrieve and provide the relevant travel-policy information. That gives the response a factual basis for matching the company rules.

exercises.question_text: The approach that retrieves relevant documents and adds them to a prompt is ___.

parts.text: The approach that retrieves relevant documents and adds them to a prompt is

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The prompt would not name the approach used to bring relevant documents into the answer.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. Do not confuse it with conversation history or with the grounded response that relevant information can support.

exercises.explanation: The term names a process that first retrieves relevant information and then augments the prompt with it. Conversation history uses earlier messages, while a grounded response is the result of using relevant supplied information.

exercises.question_text: A team lead has already asked for a summary of generative AI adoption for corporate executives. The answer is hard to scan. Which addition best solves that problem?

options.rationale: Six bullet points directly specify an easy-to-scan organization. The topic and audience are already clear, so format is the missing instruction.
A professional paragraph sample guides writing style. It does not directly make the response easier to scan.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to demonstrate a professional style. Use it when tone or wording is the main concern.

feedback.intrinsic: The summary may sound professional but remain difficult for executives to scan quickly.
feedback.instructional: The problem is organization, so request bullets, a table, or another clear structure rather than a style sample.

options.rationale: Retrieval provides relevant information for grounding a response. The stated problem is that the existing answer is hard to scan.
options.better_fit: This fits a question that lacks relevant factual information. It is useful when a response needs to be based on supplied documents.

feedback.intrinsic: The answer may gain more facts but still be presented in a hard-to-scan form.
feedback.instructional: Retrieval solves a missing-information problem. Here, add a response-structure instruction to solve the organization problem.

options.rationale: The topic and audience have already been provided. Restating them does not directly specify a more scan-friendly format.
options.better_fit: This fits a request that is vague about its topic or intended audience. It is helpful before the task has been made clear.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead may receive the same dense format even after the topic is repeated.
feedback.instructional: Because the request is already clear, focus on format. Bullet points directly improve how the response is organized.

exercises.explanation: Correct—six bullet points directly address the scanning problem. They add a clear structure without changing the established topic or audience.

exercises.question_text: A corporate communications writer has a saved message with the friendly tone needed for a new employee announcement. Which choices best help the assistant match that tone? Select all that apply.

options.text: Add the saved message as a style example
options.rationale: The saved message demonstrates the friendly tone in a concrete way. It gives a usable model for the new announcement.

options.text: Ask the model to match that style
options.rationale: This tells the model how to use the saved message. It links the style sample to the new announcement.

options.text: Request a table without a sample
options.error_type: Confuses style examples with response structure
options.rationale: A table controls organization. It does not show the friendly tone needed for the announcement.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to organize information in rows and columns. It can be combined with a style example if a table is actually needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The announcement may be organized clearly but not sound friendly to new employees.
feedback.instructional: Use a structure request for organization. Use a saved message to show the tone you want.

options.rationale: Travel-policy facts are relevant to travel-expense questions. They do not demonstrate the friendly tone of an employee announcement.
options.better_fit: This fits a travel-expense question that needs policy grounding. It does not address the requested tone.

feedback.intrinsic: The announcement may include irrelevant travel details and still miss the friendly tone.
feedback.instructional: Retrieved facts support factual answers. A saved message is the right kind of information for demonstrating tone.

exercises.explanation: Correct—the saved message shows the friendly tone, and the instruction asks the assistant to use it. This is the right use of an example in a prompt.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the following steps of RAG.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: If the prompt is sent before the information is added, the reply cannot use those facts.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Follow the dependency: retrieve the relevant information, add it to the prompt, send the prompt, then generate the grounded response.

exercises.correct_answer: Retrieve relevant information Add to prompt Send the prompt Generate a grounded response
exercises.explanation: Relevant information has to be found before it can be added to the prompt. Once the prompt includes that information, the response can use it as grounding.

exercises.question_text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more ___ than vague prompts.

parts.text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more
than vague prompts.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A vague request can lead to a response that does not match the intended task.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The missing phrase is clear and specific. Examples show style, and response structure organizes a reply, but explicit instructions make the prompt itself clear.

exercises.explanation: Explicit instructions make the requested task easier to understand than vague language. Examples and response structure can help too, but they are particular additions rather than the overall quality named here.

exercises.question_text: A support lead finds that the app gives a generic answer to a question about the current company expense policy. Which change best addresses this problem?

options.text: Retrieve policy text and add it to the prompt
options.rationale: Current policy text is relevant information for the question. Adding it to the prompt lets the response be grounded in that information.
A chat summary can preserve what has already been discussed. It may not contain the current expense-policy rules.
options.better_fit: This fits maintaining continuity in an ongoing conversation. Use it when an earlier exchange is needed for context.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may remain generic if the earlier exchange does not include the policy.
feedback.instructional: A conversation summary helps with continuity, but policy questions need relevant policy information in the prompt.

options.rationale: Bullets improve organization and scanning. They do not give the response current policy information.
options.better_fit: This fits a need for an easy-to-scan format. It can be combined with retrieved policy text.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead may get clearer bullets but the same unsupported answer.
feedback.instructional: When the problem is missing facts, add relevant retrieved information rather than only changing the format.

options.error_type: Confuses RAG with examples in prompts
options.rationale: A sample can guide the tone or style of a reply. It cannot establish what the current policy says.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to reproduce a particular writing style. Use it alongside a complete request when style matters.

feedback.intrinsic: The answer may match the desired tone but still fail to match the expense rules.
feedback.instructional: Style examples make tone concrete. Retrieved policy text provides the grounding needed here.

exercises.explanation: Correct—retrieved policy text gives the prompt current, relevant information. That directly addresses a generic policy answer.

exercises.question_text: A training coordinator needs an assistant response about privacy risks for new employees. The first prompt, “Tell me about privacy,” is too broad. Which replacement is the best fit?

options.text: Explain privacy risks for new employees in plain language
options.rationale: This request identifies the topic and the intended audience. It also asks for plain language, which gives useful style guidance.
This asks for a style sample, not an explanation of privacy risks. It does not identify new employees as the audience for the needed response.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to show a desired style after the task is already clear. It can support, but not replace, a complete request.

feedback.intrinsic: The coordinator may get a friendly sample without the privacy-risk guidance new employees need.
feedback.instructional: Start with the topic and audience. Use a style example only when you also need to make the style concrete.

options.error_type: Confuses complete specificity with structure alone
options.rationale: Three bullet points specify a format. The instruction does not say what to explain or who needs the explanation.
options.better_fit: This fits a structure request added to a complete privacy-risk prompt. It helps organize content after the task is stated.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may be short and organized but still cover the wrong subject.
feedback.instructional: Format is useful context, but it cannot replace a clear topic and audience.

options.rationale: This is broad and does not state the needed privacy topic. It also omits the intended audience and desired style.
options.better_fit: This fits a casual broad question with no specific workplace outcome. Add details when a focused explanation is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may not focus on risks or be understandable for new employees.
feedback.instructional: Make the request explicit: name the privacy risks, the audience, and the desired plain-language style.

exercises.explanation: Correct—the replacement clearly gives the topic, audience, and desired style. It is much more focused than the broad original request.

lessons.title: AI Agents Working Together · Level 1
lessons.slo: Identify the parts of an AI agent and how multiple agents can collaborate.

exercises.question_text: What does a knowledge tool provide to an agent?

options.rationale: Correct. Knowledge tools access information from sources such as search engines and databases.

options.text: A way to send an email
options.error_type: Confuses knowledge tools with action tools
options.rationale: Sending email is an external task. That task belongs to an action tool.
options.better_fit: This fits an action tool.

feedback.intrinsic: An email may be sent, but the needed facts would not be retrieved first.
feedback.instructional: Knowledge tools retrieve information; action tools perform external tasks.

options.rationale: Role and behavior are defined by instructions. A knowledge tool supplies information instead.
options.better_fit: This fits agent instructions.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent could have guidance without access to needed facts.
feedback.instructional: Instructions define behavior, while knowledge tools provide information.

options.error_type: Confuses knowledge tools with a language model
options.rationale: Language reasoning is the language model's job. A knowledge tool supplies source information.
options.better_fit: This fits the agent's large language model.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent could reason about a question but lack current records.
feedback.instructional: The language model reasons; the knowledge tool provides information.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Knowledge tools help agents find information.

exercises.question_text: Which are examples of agent tools? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. A search engine is a knowledge tool that provides information.
Correct. A database can provide information to an agent.
Correct. Updating a calendar is an external task performed through an action tool.
A system prompt defines role and behavior. It is not a capability for world interaction.
options.better_fit: This fits agent instructions.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent would know how to behave but could not retrieve information or update a calendar.
feedback.instructional: Tools provide world-facing capabilities; instructions provide guidance.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Agent tools include both information and action capabilities.

exercises.question_text: A knowledge tool is mainly used to directly send emails or control devices.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The needed information may never be found before external action is attempted.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Knowledge tools retrieve information; action tools send emails or control devices.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Those are action-tool tasks, not information-retrieval tasks.

exercises.question_text: Agent tools are capabilities that let an agent interact with the world.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The agent would be limited to language responses without information or external work.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Agent tools provide capabilities for world interaction.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Tools connect an agent to information and external actions.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe an agent's large language model? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is the agent's brain for language understanding
options.rationale: Correct. The language model is the brain-like element for understanding language.

options.text: It supports reasoning over natural language
options.rationale: Correct. It helps the agent reason about natural-language input.

options.text: It defines the agent's role and behavior
options.rationale: Role and behavior are defined by instructions. The language model provides language reasoning instead.
options.better_fit: This fits agent instructions.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant could understand a request but lack role guidance.
feedback.instructional: Keep instructions separate from the language model.

options.text: It directly sends emails and updates calendars
options.error_type: Confuses the model with action tools
options.rationale: Email and calendar changes are external actions. They require action tools rather than the language model alone.
options.better_fit: This fits action tools.

feedback.intrinsic: The external task would not be performed by reasoning alone.
feedback.instructional: The language model reasons; action tools carry out external tasks.

exercises.explanation: Correct! The language model provides language understanding and reasoning.

exercises.question_text: What do agent instructions define?

options.rationale: Correct. Instructions define the agent's role and behavior.

options.error_type: Confuses instructions with the language model
options.rationale: Language reasoning comes from the large language model. Instructions specify behavior instead.
options.better_fit: This fits the agent's large language model.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent could have behavior guidance but still need reasoning ability.
feedback.instructional: Instructions are the job description; the language model is the reasoning component.

options.error_type: Confuses instructions with a knowledge tool
options.rationale: A database supplies information through a knowledge tool. Instructions do not contain or retrieve those facts.
options.better_fit: This fits a knowledge tool connected to a database.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent could know its role but lack the required facts.
feedback.instructional: Instructions guide behavior; knowledge tools provide information.

options.text: The external tasks a tool performs
options.rationale: Action tools perform external tasks. Instructions define how the agent should behave.
options.better_fit: This fits an action tool.

feedback.intrinsic: The requested calendar or email action might remain unperformed.
feedback.instructional: Instructions guide work; action tools carry out external work.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Instructions work like the agent's job description.

exercises.question_text: A large language model helps an AI agent understand and reason over natural language.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The agent could not reliably work through a language request.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A large language model helps an agent understand and reason over natural language.

exercises.explanation: Correct! That is the language model's brain-like role.

exercises.question_text: Agent instructions are action tools that send emails or update calendars.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: An email or calendar request would not be completed merely by setting guidance.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Instructions are a system prompt that defines role and behavior; action tools perform tasks.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Instructions guide behavior, while action tools perform external tasks.

exercises.question_text: What is an AI agent?

options.text: A generative AI application that reasons, uses tools, and takes action
options.rationale: Correct. An AI agent combines language reasoning, tools, and context-sensitive action.

options.text: A model that only generates natural-language text
options.error_type: Confuses an agent with a language model
options.rationale: This describes language generation alone. An agent can also use tools and act.
options.better_fit: This fits a language model used only to generate text.

feedback.intrinsic: The requested work could remain unfinished.
feedback.instructional: An agent is more than a text-generating model because it can use tools and take action.

options.text: A set of instructions that defines a role
options.rationale: Instructions guide an agent's behavior. They are not the complete application.
options.better_fit: This fits agent instructions or a system prompt.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant would have guidance but no complete way to perform work.
feedback.instructional: Instructions are one agent element; they do not replace the agent.

options.text: A group of specialized collaborating agents
options.error_type: Confuses an agent with a multi-agent system
options.rationale: A multi-agent system contains several agents. An AI agent can be one member of that group.
options.better_fit: This fits a multi-agent system.

feedback.intrinsic: You would design several specialists for a one-assistant need.
feedback.instructional: An individual AI agent differs from a collaborating group of agents.

exercises.explanation: Correct! An AI agent reasons, uses tools, and can take appropriate action.

exercises.question_text: Which statements are true about action tools and multi-agent systems? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Sending email is an external task an action tool can perform.
Correct. Updating a calendar is another external action.

options.text: Specialized agents can collaborate on a workflow
options.rationale: Correct. Multi-agent systems coordinate specialized agents on shared work.
Knowledge tools retrieve information. Device control is an external action.
options.better_fit: This fits an action tool.

feedback.intrinsic: A device-control request could be assigned to retrieval and never completed.
feedback.instructional: Knowledge tools find information; action tools perform tasks such as device control.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Action tools perform tasks, and specialized agents can collaborate.

exercises.question_text: An AI agent only answers questions and cannot use tools to automate tasks.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A request needing an email or calendar update could remain incomplete.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: AI agents can reason over language, use tools, and respond with appropriate action.

exercises.explanation: Correct! An AI agent can use tools to automate tasks.

exercises.question_text: In a multi-agent system, agents can communicate through prompts to decide tasks and responsibility.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Specialists could duplicate work or leave tasks unassigned.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Multi-agent systems use prompts to communicate about needed tasks and responsibility.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Prompts can help agents coordinate tasks and responsibility.
