lessons.title: Tokens and Text Preparation · Level 1
lessons.slo: Prepare text for analysis by using tokenization and common preprocessing methods.

exercises.question_text: What is a corpus in NLP?

options.text: A body of text for analysis
options.rationale: A corpus is the body of language content being analyzed. It is the starting collection before it is broken into tokens.
Normalization can change punctuation or letter case before tokens are generated. It does not define the full body of content being analyzed.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing content after surface differences have been standardized.

feedback.intrinsic: You would mistake a preparation result for the full collection of content.
feedback.instructional: A corpus is the whole body of content; normalization is only one possible preparation step.

options.rationale: A sequence of terms treated as one group is an n-gram. A corpus can contain many such sequences.
options.better_fit: This fits when naming a phrase such as a two-word bigram or three-word trigram.

feedback.intrinsic: You would label one small phrase as though it were the entire collection.
feedback.instructional: An n-gram is a grouped sequence of terms, while a corpus is the body of content under analysis.

options.text: A grammatical label for a word
options.rationale: A grammatical label such as noun or verb comes from POS tagging. It describes an individual token, not the collection being analyzed.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying a token’s grammatical category.

feedback.intrinsic: You would focus on one token’s grammar instead of the collection to prepare.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging labels tokens; a corpus is the body of content containing those tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A corpus is the body of content selected for analysis.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about n-grams are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A unigram is a one-word phrase treated as a group. It is the one-term form of an n-gram.
A bigram is a sequence of two terms treated as a group. Multi-term groups can preserve phrase meaning.
A trigram has three words. A two-word sequence is a bigram.
options.better_fit: This fits if “trigram” is replaced with “bigram.”

feedback.intrinsic: You would assign the wrong group size to a phrase.
feedback.instructional: Remember the counts: unigram is one, bigram is two, and trigram is three.

options.rationale: Removing endings such as “ing” and “ed” is stemming. An n-gram groups a sequence of terms.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing stemming.

feedback.intrinsic: You would change word forms instead of preserving a meaningful sequence.
feedback.instructional: N-grams group terms; stemming strips endings to consolidate related forms.

exercises.explanation: Correct. N-grams are grouped sequences, and their names indicate the number of terms.

exercises.question_text: Tokenization can create tokens from whole words, partial words, or combinations of words and punctuation.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Treating tokens as words only can miss how punctuation and word parts are represented.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Tokenization can produce whole words, partial words, or combinations of words and punctuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Tokens are not limited to whole words.

exercises.question_text: A bigram is a sequence of three terms treated as a group.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Using three terms would place the phrase in the wrong n-gram category.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A unigram has one word, a bigram has two, and a trigram has three.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A bigram has two terms.

exercises.question_text: Which method strips endings such as “ing” and “ed” to group related forms?

options.rationale: Stemming strips endings such as “s,” “ing,” and “ed.” It consolidates related forms under a shared root.
Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return a valid dictionary base form. It does more than simply chop endings.
options.better_fit: This fits when a valid lemma such as “run” is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: You might expect a valid dictionary form when only ending stripping is being described.
feedback.instructional: Stemming strips endings; lemmatization uses rules and vocabulary to produce a valid word.

options.rationale: Normalization can lowercase words or remove punctuation. It does not strip endings to group related forms.
options.better_fit: This fits when standardizing case or punctuation before token generation.

feedback.intrinsic: Related forms could remain separate during counting.
feedback.instructional: Use stemming to consolidate endings such as “ing” and “ed”; normalization handles surface differences.

options.rationale: POS tagging labels a token as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb. It does not alter word endings.
options.better_fit: This fits when grammatical categories are required.

feedback.intrinsic: You would add grammar labels without grouping the related word forms.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging classifies grammar; stemming strips endings.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Stemming groups related forms by stripping endings.

exercises.question_text: Which actions are text normalization? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Removing punctuation is a surface-form standardization. It can help analysis based purely on word frequency.
Changing case standardizes surface differences before token generation. This can improve frequency-based analysis.

options.error_type: Confuses normalization with stop word removal
options.rationale: Excluding common words is stop word removal. Normalization instead standardizes features such as punctuation and capitalization.
options.better_fit: This fits when low-meaning common words should be removed to reveal content words.

feedback.intrinsic: You would remove words rather than standardize their surface form.
feedback.instructional: Stop word removal excludes words like “the”; normalization can lowercase words or remove punctuation.

options.text: Use grammar rules for base forms
options.rationale: Using linguistic rules and vocabulary to produce a valid base form is lemmatization. Normalization does not perform that dictionary-form reduction.
options.better_fit: This fits when a valid lemma such as “run” is required.

feedback.intrinsic: You would change word forms when the task only calls for surface standardization.
feedback.instructional: Lemmatization uses rules and vocabulary; normalization handles case and punctuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Both actions standardize surface differences before token generation.

exercises.question_text: POS tagging can label a token as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb by using the token and its context.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Ignoring context can lead to the wrong grammatical category for a token.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: POS tagging labels tokens as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb and uses both the token and its sentence context.

exercises.explanation: Correct. POS tagging assigns grammatical categories using the token and its context.

exercises.question_text: Which word is a common stop word?

options.rationale: “The” is a common word that helps people read but often adds little semantic meaning. It is a standard stop-word example.
This is a two-term phrase that can be treated as a bigram. It is not a common low-meaning word.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying a meaningful two-word n-gram.

feedback.intrinsic: You would remove a phrase that may identify a main topic.
feedback.instructional: Stop words are common words such as “the,” “a,” and “it,” not meaningful multi-term phrases.

options.error_type: Confuses stop words with a word form
options.rationale: “Running” is a word form that can be reduced to “run” by lemmatization. It is not identified as a common stop word.
options.better_fit: This fits when discussing a word that lemmatization can reduce to a valid base form.

feedback.intrinsic: You could remove a content word instead of preparing its form.
feedback.instructional: Stop word removal targets common low-meaning words; “running” is used to illustrate lemmatization.

options.error_type: Confuses stop words with punctuation-sensitive token
options.rationale: “Banks.” may differ from “banks” because the period signals sentence position. It is not a listed common stop word.
options.better_fit: This fits when preserving punctuation-sensitive meaning is important.

feedback.intrinsic: You would discard a token whose punctuation may carry useful meaning.
feedback.instructional: Stop words are common readability words; punctuation-sensitive terms can need to be retained.

exercises.explanation: Correct. “The” often adds little semantic meaning and may be excluded.

exercises.question_text: Text normalization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return valid dictionary forms.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would substitute base-form reduction for surface standardization.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return a valid dictionary form. Normalization can lowercase words or remove punctuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. That process is lemmatization, not normalization.

exercises.question_text: Stop word removal changes every word to lowercase before analysis.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would use the wrong preparation method for common-word removal.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Stop word removal excludes words such as “the,” “a,” and “it.” Changing case is text normalization.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lowercasing is a normalization action.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The timing of the preparation action is no longer clear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Name normalization, state its action, then show that it can happen before tokens are generated.

exercises.correct_answer: Text normalization can remove punctuation before tokens are generated
exercises.explanation: Normalization is a preparation choice that can occur before token generation, so the timing phrase follows the action.

exercises.question_text: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” are often called ___.

parts.text: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” are often called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The label would confuse common low-meaning words with units, phrases, or dictionary base forms.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Tokens are units, n-grams are term sequences, and lemmas are valid base forms. “The,” “a,” and “it” are stop words.

exercises.explanation: These common readability words often add little semantic meaning, so they may be excluded to highlight content words.

flashcards.back: It breaks a corpus into tokens.
It standardizes text, such as lowercase words or removed punctuation.
Common words that often add little semantic meaning.
A two-word sequence treated as a group.

lessons.title: Tokens and Text Preparation · Level 2
lessons.slo: Prepare text for analysis by using tokenization and common preprocessing methods.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe lemmatization? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Lemmatization uses linguistic rules to reduce a word to its base form. Those rules help ensure the result is valid.
Lemmatization uses vocabulary as well as linguistic rules. This supports valid dictionary forms.
Simply chopping endings describes stemming. Lemmatization uses rules and vocabulary instead.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing stemming.

feedback.intrinsic: You could produce a form that is not a valid word.
feedback.instructional: Lemmatization aims for a valid dictionary form, not merely an ending-stripped form.

options.rationale: Labeling nouns and verbs is POS tagging. Lemmatization reduces words to valid base forms.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing POS tagging.

feedback.intrinsic: You would classify grammar instead of finding the required base form.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging assigns grammatical categories; lemmatization returns a lemma.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to produce valid dictionary base forms.

exercises.question_text: Removing stop words can help identify important content words.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Common readability words can continue to hide the terms that carry the main topics.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” often add little semantic meaning, so excluding them can highlight content words.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Removing common low-meaning words can make important terms easier to identify.

exercises.question_text: Order the pieces correctly.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The definition no longer clearly identifies what an n-gram groups.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the term, then link it to “a sequence” and finish with what the sequence contains.

exercises.correct_answer: An n-gram is a sequence of terms
exercises.explanation: The definition links the name n-gram to its core idea: a sequence of terms treated together.

exercises.question_text: Breaking a body of text into tokens is called ___.

parts.text: Breaking a body of text into tokens is called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The chosen method would not perform the initial split into units.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Normalization standardizes surface form, n-gram extraction groups sequences, and POS tagging adds grammar labels. Tokenization is the splitting step.

exercises.explanation: Tokenization creates the individual units that can then be counted or prepared in other ways.

exercises.question_text: A customer-message analyst wants phrase meanings to remain clear during analysis. Which phrases should the analyst treat as n-grams? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is a multi-term phrase that can be treated as one group. Grouping it can preserve meaning that separate words may miss.
This three-term phrase is a trigram. Treating it as a group can preserve its phrase meaning.

options.error_type: Confuses a stop word with a multi-term phrase
options.rationale: “The” is a common stop word and contains only one word. It does not illustrate a multi-term phrase needing grouping.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying a common word that may be excluded.

feedback.intrinsic: You would group a common readability word instead of a meaningful phrase.
feedback.instructional: Use n-grams for multi-term sequences; “the” is commonly treated as a stop word.

options.rationale: “Running” becoming “run” describes lemmatization. It is not a phrase selected because its terms form one meaning group.
options.better_fit: This fits when showing a valid dictionary base-form conversion.

feedback.intrinsic: You would confuse word-form reduction with phrase grouping.
feedback.instructional: Lemmatization reduces a word to a lemma; n-grams group terms that appear together.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Grouping these phrases can retain meaning that individual words may not show.

exercises.question_text: A support analyst receives thousands of customer support tickets and must count the terms used in them. What should the analyst do first?

options.rationale: Counting terms requires identifiable token units. Tokenization breaks the collection into those units first.
Two-word phrases are bigrams, which are grouped sequences of terms. The terms must first be available as tokens.
options.better_fit: This fits when preserving the meaning of a two-term phrase is the goal.

feedback.intrinsic: Term counting would begin with only selected phrase groups instead of the basic units.
feedback.instructional: Start by tokenizing; use n-grams later when grouped phrases matter.

options.error_type: Confuses tokenization with stop word removal
options.rationale: Stop word removal excludes common low-meaning words. It is not the step that breaks content into countable units.
options.better_fit: This fits when important content words need to stand out.

feedback.intrinsic: You could discard words before first creating the units needed for counting.
feedback.instructional: Tokenization creates tokens; stop word removal is a later choice for focusing on content words.

options.rationale: POS tagging assigns categories such as noun or verb using context. Grammar labels are not needed to create countable tokens.
options.better_fit: This fits when grammatical categories are needed.

feedback.intrinsic: You would spend effort adding grammar labels instead of preparing countable units.
feedback.instructional: Tokenization comes first because it breaks the collection into tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Tokenization provides the units whose frequencies can be counted.

exercises.question_text: Changing all words to lowercase before token generation is text ___.

parts.text: Changing all words to lowercase before token generation is text

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The selected method would change which words are included or how their forms are reduced instead of standardizing case.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Stop word removal excludes common words, stemming strips endings, and lemmatization finds valid base forms. Lowercasing is normalization.

exercises.explanation: Lowercasing standardizes a surface difference while leaving the word content available for frequency analysis.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The process and the kind of information it assigns are no longer connected clearly.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Begin with POS tagging, then show that it labels each token with a grammatical category.

exercises.correct_answer: POS tagging labels each token with a grammatical category
exercises.explanation: POS tagging acts on each token and assigns a grammatical category such as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.

exercises.question_text: A customer-feedback analyst is counting terms and does not need capitalization or punctuation details. Which preparation actions should the analyst choose? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Lowercasing standardizes case when capitalization details are not needed. It supports frequency-based counting.
Removing punctuation is suitable when its meaning is not needed. It standardizes content for frequency-based analysis.
A period can carry sentence-ending information, but that detail is not needed here. The stated goal is term counting without punctuation details.
options.better_fit: This fits when sentence-ending punctuation must remain meaningful.

feedback.intrinsic: You would keep a detail the analyst has said is unnecessary for counting terms.
feedback.instructional: Preserve punctuation when it matters; otherwise normalization can remove it for frequency-based analysis.

options.rationale: Valid dictionary base forms require lemmatization. The stated need is only to standardize capitalization and punctuation.
options.better_fit: This fits when words such as “running” must become the valid form “run.”

feedback.intrinsic: You would add base-form processing that does not address the stated surface differences.
feedback.instructional: Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary; lowercase and punctuation changes are normalization.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These choices standardize the details that the analyst does not need.

exercises.question_text: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” are often called ___.

parts.text: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” are often called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The label would confuse common low-meaning words with units, phrases, or dictionary base forms.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Tokens are units, n-grams are term sequences, and lemmas are valid base forms. “The,” “a,” and “it” are stop words.

exercises.explanation: These common readability words often add little semantic meaning, so they may be excluded to highlight content words.

exercises.question_text: A text analyst needs “running” to become the valid dictionary word “run” before analyzing customer feedback. Which method should the analyst use?

options.rationale: Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return valid dictionary base forms. “Running” to “run” is its stated behavior.

options.error_type: Confuses valid lemma with stripped stem
options.rationale: Stemming strips endings to group related forms. Its result may not be a valid word.
options.better_fit: This fits when consolidating related forms without needing a guaranteed valid dictionary result.

feedback.intrinsic: The analyst may not receive the required valid dictionary word.
feedback.instructional: Choose lemmatization when the result must be a valid lemma such as “run.”

options.rationale: Normalization standardizes punctuation or capitalization. It does not use vocabulary and rules to return “run.”
options.better_fit: This fits when case or punctuation should be standardized before token generation.

feedback.intrinsic: “Running” could remain unchanged as a word form.
feedback.instructional: Normalization handles surface differences; lemmatization reduces a word to a valid base form.

options.error_type: Confuses base-form reduction with phrase grouping
options.rationale: N-gram extraction groups sequences of terms. It does not change a word to its dictionary base form.
options.better_fit: This fits when a multi-term phrase should be treated as a group.

feedback.intrinsic: The needed base form would not be produced.
feedback.instructional: Use lemmatization for valid base forms and n-grams for grouped term sequences.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lemmatization returns the valid dictionary base form required here.

exercises.question_text: An employee-feedback analyst needs the main topics in comments. Which step should the analyst use to make content words easier to identify?

options.rationale: Removing common low-meaning words can make content words easier to identify. That directly supports finding main topics.

options.error_type: Confuses stop word removal with normalization
options.rationale: Lowercasing standardizes case for frequency-based analysis. It does not remove common readability words.
options.better_fit: This fits when capitalization differences should not affect term counts.

feedback.intrinsic: Common words could still obscure the main topics.
feedback.instructional: Use stop word removal to exclude low-meaning words; use lowercasing to standardize case.

options.error_type: Confuses stop word removal with n-gram extraction
options.rationale: Bigrams preserve the meaning of two-term sequences. They do not remove common words that can hide content terms.
options.better_fit: This fits when a two-word phrase should be treated as a group.

feedback.intrinsic: Frequent common words may remain mixed with the important terms.
feedback.instructional: N-grams group sequences; stop word removal makes content words easier to identify.

options.rationale: Counting occurrences is frequency analysis after tokens are prepared. It does not itself exclude low-meaning words.
options.better_fit: This fits when measuring how often each normalized token appears.

feedback.intrinsic: The count could remain dominated by common readability words.
feedback.instructional: Remove stop words first when the goal is to make important content words stand out.

exercises.explanation: Correct. This removes common words that often add little semantic meaning.

exercises.question_text: What is “natural language processing” when treated as one group?

exercises.question_text: What is TextRank?

options.rationale: TextRank represents connected text units in a graph and ranks them. It works without labeled training examples.

options.text: A supervised classifier trained on labeled examples
options.rationale: TextRank does not learn from labeled examples. It calculates importance from graph connections.
options.better_fit: This fits a model trained to assign labels such as topic or sentiment.

options.text: A frequency-analysis method that only counts words
options.error_type: Confuses graph ranking with frequency analysis
options.rationale: Frequency analysis counts occurrences rather than ranking graph nodes. TextRank uses relationships among text units.
options.better_fit: This fits a task requiring simple counts of repeated terms.

options.text: An abstractive system that writes new summary sentences
options.rationale: TextRank ranks existing units such as sentences or words. Writing new language is an abstractive approach.
options.better_fit: This fits a summary task where generated wording is allowed.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TextRank is an unsupervised graph-ranking algorithm.

exercises.question_text: In sentence-level TextRank, select the correct statements.

options.rationale: Sentence-level TextRank represents each sentence as a graph node. Nodes are the items being ranked.
Edges link the sentence nodes. They represent relationships between sentences.

options.text: Edge weights can represent sentence similarity.
options.rationale: Weights indicate how strongly two sentence nodes relate. Word overlap or cosine similarity can supply those values.

options.text: Each sentence is automatically a keyword.
options.rationale: Sentences are nodes in sentence-level TextRank. Keywords are high-ranked words in word-level TextRank.
options.better_fit: This fits word-level TextRank output after ranking word nodes.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Sentences are nodes connected by similarity-weighted edges.

options.better_fit: This fits an abstractive summarizer that may create new language.

options.text: Replace edge weights with word counts
options.error_type: Confuses ranking output with graph construction
options.rationale: Edge weights are part of the graph before ranking converges. They are not replaced after scoring.
options.better_fit: This fits a separate frequency-analysis procedure.

options.text: Treat each sentence as a keyword
options.error_type: Confuses sentence summaries with keyword extraction
options.rationale: Sentence-level TextRank selects sentences for summaries. Keyword extraction ranks word nodes instead.
options.better_fit: This fits a word-level keyword-extraction task.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Top-ranked original sentences are selected.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe TextRank? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: TextRank ranks nodes that represent text units. Their connections contribute to importance scores.
TextRank adapts PageRank's core ranking idea to text graphs. Connected important nodes reinforce one another.
TextRank does not require a labeled training set. It derives rankings from the graph structure.

options.text: It requires labeled examples before ranking text.
options.rationale: Labeled examples are not required for TextRank. The algorithm ranks text from graph relationships.
options.better_fit: This fits supervised models that learn predictions from annotated data.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TextRank is graph-based, PageRank-like, and unsupervised.

exercises.question_text: How does word-level TextRank extract keywords? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Words are the nodes in word-level TextRank. The algorithm ranks them in a co-occurrence graph.

options.text: Link words that co-occur within a fixed window.
options.rationale: Nearby co-occurring words receive connections. Those connections form the word graph.

options.text: Select the highest-ranked words as key terms.
options.rationale: After ranking, the highest-ranked word nodes are extracted. They represent the main topics.

options.text: Rank words only by raw frequency.
options.rationale: Raw counting alone is frequency analysis. TextRank uses graph connections and graph-based ranking.
options.better_fit: This fits finding the most frequently occurring tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TextRank links co-occurring word nodes and ranks them.

options.better_fit: This fits revising a graph when the similarity method changes.

feedback.intrinsic: The system would delay the required sentence selection.
feedback.instructional: After convergence, select the highest-ranked sentences.

options.better_fit: This fits selecting important original sentences from the comments.

feedback.intrinsic: The output would be sentences rather than topic terms.
feedback.instructional: Use the word-level TextRank graph for keyword extraction.

options.rationale: Frequency analysis counts repeated words but does not model word co-occurrence links. The scenario explicitly requires graph-based ranking of nearby words.
options.better_fit: This fits a simple count of the most repeated terms.

feedback.intrinsic: The analyst would lose the co-occurrence relationship required by the task.
feedback.instructional: TextRank uses a co-occurrence graph to rank key terms.

feedback.instructional: TextRank uses graph links between text units.

options.better_fit: This fits producing a newly worded summary.

feedback.instructional: Choose TextRank when ranking connected sentences is the goal.

exercises.question_text: A writer is building a TextRank graph for five report sentences. Which choices should the writer make? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Sentence-level TextRank represents every sentence with a node. These nodes are then ranked.

options.text: Use word overlap to estimate similarity.
options.rationale: Word overlap is one common way to estimate sentence similarity. Its result can provide an edge weight.

options.rationale: One sentence's word count does not compare a sentence pair. An edge should encode their relationship.
options.better_fit: This fits a simple frequency-analysis report for individual sentences.

feedback.instructional: Use a similarity measure such as word overlap for edge weights.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Sentence nodes and similarity-weighted edges form the graph.

exercises.question_text: What is TextRank?

options.rationale: TextRank represents connected text units in a graph and ranks them. It works without labeled training examples.

options.text: A supervised classifier trained on labeled examples
options.rationale: TextRank does not learn from labeled examples. It calculates importance from graph connections.
options.better_fit: This fits a model trained to assign labels such as topic or sentiment.

options.text: A frequency-analysis method that only counts words
options.error_type: Confuses graph ranking with frequency analysis
options.rationale: Frequency analysis counts occurrences rather than ranking graph nodes. TextRank uses relationships among text units.
options.better_fit: This fits a task requiring simple counts of repeated terms.

options.text: An abstractive system that writes new summary sentences
options.rationale: TextRank ranks existing units such as sentences or words. Writing new language is an abstractive approach.
options.better_fit: This fits a summary task where generated wording is allowed.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TextRank is an unsupervised graph-ranking algorithm.

exercises.question_text: Which steps belong to TextRank sentence summarization? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: TextRank iteratively recalculates node ranks. Connected nodes and weighted edges influence those updates.
The updates continue until the ranks settle. Convergence indicates stable scores.
The highest-ranked original sentences are selected for an extractive summary. Selection follows the ranking process.
TextRank selects original sentences rather than composing new ones. New language is characteristic of abstractive summarization.
options.better_fit: This fits an abstractive summary that paraphrases key themes.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TextRank iterates ranks, waits for convergence, and selects top sentences.

exercises.question_text: TextRank can rank connected sentences or words without labeled training data.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: You would exclude a method that can work without labels.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: TextRank ranks connected text units using an unsupervised graph-based approach.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TextRank is unsupervised.

exercises.question_text: Abstractive summarization generates new language that conveys key themes.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: You would reject the defining feature of an abstractive summary.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Abstractive methods generate wording, whereas extractive methods select it.

exercises.explanation: Correct. New language distinguishes abstractive summaries.

exercises.question_text: What does an edge weight commonly measure in sentence-level TextRank?

options.rationale: An edge weight expresses how similar two connected sentences are. It can be based on word overlap or cosine similarity.

options.error_type: Confuses pairwise similarity with sentence length
options.rationale: Sentence length describes one node, not the relationship between two nodes. Edge weights compare connected sentences.
options.better_fit: This fits a feature that measures individual sentence length.

options.text: The final rank of a sentence
options.error_type: Confuses edge weights with node ranks
options.rationale: Ranks belong to nodes after iterative updates. Edge weights are inputs describing connections.
options.better_fit: This fits the importance score assigned to a node after ranking.

options.text: The number of keywords in the document
options.error_type: Confuses sentence edges with keyword output
options.rationale: Keyword counts do not describe a pair of sentence nodes. An edge weight represents their similarity.
options.better_fit: This fits a report about extracted keyword quantity.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Edge weights measure sentence similarity.

exercises.question_text: A legal analyst must choose a method for a contract brief where every output sentence must come verbatim from the contract. Which decisions best satisfy that constraint? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Extractive summarization selects source sentences rather than generating them. It therefore preserves verbatim wording.

options.text: Use TextRank to rank source sentences before selecting them.
options.rationale: TextRank can rank the importance of source sentences. Selecting its top sentences remains an extractive process.

options.text: Check that each selected sentence appears in the contract.
options.rationale: This validation directly tests the verbatim constraint. It helps ensure no generated wording enters the brief.

options.text: Use abstractive summarization to paraphrase obligations.
options.error_type: Confuses generated language with source selection
options.rationale: Abstractive summarization generates language that may not appear in the contract. That conflicts with the verbatim requirement.
options.better_fit: This fits a reader-friendly explanation where paraphrasing is allowed.

feedback.intrinsic: The brief could contain sentences not found in the contract.
feedback.instructional: A verbatim constraint requires extractive sentence selection.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The constraint favors extractive sentence selection and source verification.

options.text: Edge weights can represent sentence similarity.

options.text: Each sentence is automatically a keyword.
options.rationale: Sentences are nodes in sentence-level TextRank. Keywords are high-ranked words in word-level TextRank.
options.better_fit: This fits word-level TextRank output after ranking word nodes.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Sentences are nodes connected by similarity-weighted edges.

lessons.title: Meaning with Embeddings · Level 1
lessons.slo: Use embeddings and vector relationships to explain semantic text analysis.

exercises.question_text: Which tasks can semantic embeddings support? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Embeddings can identify sentences central to overall meaning. Those existing sentences can be selected as a summary.
Word vectors can be compared with a document vector. Semantically central words can become keywords.
Token embeddings in context can support recognizing entities. Context helps distinguish entity roles.
Punctuation removal is a preprocessing operation. It is not a semantic embedding application.
options.better_fit: Use punctuation removal when normalizing text before analysis.

feedback.intrinsic: Text would be prepared but no meaning-based task would be completed.
feedback.instructional: Embeddings support semantic tasks such as summarization and entity recognition.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Semantic embeddings can support summarization, keywords, and entity recognition.

exercises.question_text: What do semantic language models encode?

options.rationale: Semantic language models encode relationships among language tokens. Those relationships enable machines to work with meaning.
Frequency counts measure occurrence, not relationships in meaning. They do not produce semantic token representations.
options.better_fit: Use frequency counts when identifying commonly occurring terms.

feedback.intrinsic: Related words would remain separate counts.
feedback.instructional: Semantic models represent relationships in meaning, not only frequency.

options.rationale: Grammatical labels identify roles such as noun or verb. They do not encode semantic relationships between tokens.
options.better_fit: Use POS tagging when a token's grammatical category is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: You would get a grammar label instead of semantic relationships.
feedback.instructional: Semantic models focus on meaning relationships.

options.rationale: Graph edges connect nodes in a TextRank-style graph. Semantic language models encode token relationships as vectors.
options.better_fit: Use sentence-graph edges when ranking sentences for extractive summarization.

feedback.intrinsic: You would select a graph structure rather than a token representation.
feedback.instructional: Graphs rank nodes; semantic models encode token meaning.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These models encode relationships between language tokens.

exercises.question_text: Semantic keyword extraction finds key terms by comparing only how often each word appears.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Important but less frequent meaning-bearing terms could be missed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Semantic extraction uses vector relationships, not frequency alone.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Semantic keyword extraction compares word vectors with a document representation.

exercises.question_text: Word2Vec and GloVe represent tokens as dense vectors with many numeric dimensions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The numeric representation would be overlooked.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Word2Vec and GloVe use dense vectors with many dimensions.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Their representations are dense, multi-dimensional numeric vectors.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe an embedding? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is a multi-valued numeric vector.
options.rationale: An embedding contains multiple numeric values. Together they represent a language token.

options.text: It represents a token in multidimensional space.
options.rationale: A vector can be treated as a point in multidimensional space. Embeddings use this representation for tokens.
Embeddings depend on numeric dimensions. Those values determine vector relationships.
options.better_fit: Use a simple category label when no vector representation is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: There would be no vector orientation to compare.
feedback.instructional: Embeddings are numeric and multi-dimensional.

options.text: It is only a count of occurrences.
options.rationale: Occurrence counts are frequency features. An embedding is a vector representation rather than a count.
options.better_fit: Use word counts in bag-of-words feature extraction.

feedback.intrinsic: Meaning relationships would not be represented.
feedback.instructional: Keep count-based features separate from embeddings.

exercises.explanation: Correct. An embedding is a numeric vector representing a token.

exercises.question_text: Which parts appear in the cosine similarity formula? Select all that apply.

options.text: The dot product of A and B
options.rationale: The dot product is the numerator of the formula. It combines the two vectors' dimensions.
The magnitude of A is in the denominator. It normalizes the directional comparison.
The magnitude of B is also in the denominator. Both magnitudes are required.
Document count is used by inverse document frequency. Cosine similarity uses two vectors, their dot product, and magnitudes.
options.better_fit: Use document count when calculating inverse document frequency.

feedback.intrinsic: A corpus-wide count would be mixed into a two-vector calculation.
feedback.instructional: Cosine similarity does not use a document count.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The formula uses a dot product and both vector magnitudes.

exercises.question_text: Semantically similar words usually have vectors pointing in very different directions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Related words would be placed as unrelated directions.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Semantic similarity is generally reflected by similar, not very different, directions.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Similar meanings tend to have similar vector orientations.

exercises.question_text: What does attention calculate for a token?

options.rationale: Attention calculates the influence of surrounding tokens. That influence shapes a contextualized representation.
Occurrence frequency is a count-based feature. Attention calculates contextual influence.
options.better_fit: Use frequency analysis to count token occurrences.

feedback.intrinsic: Changing meaning across contexts would be missed.
feedback.instructional: Attention focuses on surrounding-token influence.

options.rationale: POS tagging assigns grammatical categories. Attention builds a context-aware representation.
options.better_fit: Use POS tagging to label nouns, verbs, or adjectives.

feedback.intrinsic: You would obtain a grammar label instead of a contextual representation.
feedback.instructional: Attention is about contextual influence.

options.rationale: Graph edge counts concern network relationships. Attention measures the influence of surrounding tokens.
options.better_fit: Use graph edges when ranking connected nodes in TextRank.

feedback.intrinsic: You would rank graph connections rather than capture context.
feedback.instructional: Attention shapes token representations using context.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Attention evaluates how nearby tokens influence a representation.

exercises.question_text: A high cosine similarity means two vectors have similar orientations.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Aligned vectors would be treated as unrelated.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Cosine similarity measures directional orientation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A high score signals similar vector directions.

exercises.question_text: Which vector operations are shown by the animal examples? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Adding young transforms dog toward puppy. It represents an adult-to-young relationship.
The same transformation maps cat toward kitten. The relationship is encoded as vector arithmetic.
Subtracting young reverses the transformation. It returns from puppy toward dog.
Tree does not represent the young transformation. The examples use young to connect adult and young animals.
options.better_fit: Use tree when comparing its similarity with animal words.

feedback.intrinsic: The adult-to-young relationship would be lost.
feedback.instructional: Use young as the semantic transformation vector.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Adding or subtracting young moves between adult and young-animal relationships.

exercises.question_text: Contextualized embeddings let a token's representation reflect its surrounding context.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Nearby words would be treated as irrelevant.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Contextualized embeddings reflect context through attention.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Attention uses surrounding tokens to shape the representation.

exercises.question_text: Vector arithmetic requires the resulting vector to exactly match a word vector in real systems.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Useful near matches could be rejected.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Exact matches are uncommon; retrieve the closest vector instead.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Real systems usually retrieve the closest vector.

Surrounding tokens that influence a token's representation.

exercises.question_text: A product team compares embeddings for dog, cat, and tree. Which findings support expected semantic relationships? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dog and cat can have similar directions.
options.rationale: Dog and cat are semantically related. Related terms tend to have similarly oriented vectors.

options.text: Tree can be less related to dog.
options.rationale: Tree is less semantically related to dog than cat is. Its orientation can therefore be less similar.
Semantic similarity does not require identical vectors. Tree is also less related to the animal terms.

feedback.instructional: Related words can be similar without being identical.

options.text: Meaning comes only from word counts.

options.rationale: Graph edges connect nodes in a TextRank-style graph. Semantic language models encode token relationships as vectors.

feedback.intrinsic: You would select a graph structure rather than a token representation.

exercises.question_text: What does speech recognition do? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Recognition takes spoken language as input. It begins with captured speech.
Producing written text from speech is recognition's core role. It is therefore called speech-to-text.
A transcription gives an app usable written content. That supports understanding a spoken request.
Reading text aloud is speech synthesis. Recognition moves from speech to text instead.

feedback.intrinsic: No written transcript would be produced.

options.better_fit: It fits audio-capture quality requirements.

feedback.intrinsic: Clearer audio would not supply text access.
feedback.instructional: Accessibility concerns user needs and alternative methods.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Accessibility designs for different user needs.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Spoken articles provide an alternative way to consume written content for people with dyslexia.

exercises.question_text: What can speech synthesis create for a game?

options.rationale: Correct. Creators can use synthesis to generate character voices for games and interactive experiences.

options.error_type: Confuses media synthesis with call recognition
options.rationale: A call record is written text produced from spoken customer calls. A character voice is generated audio.
options.better_fit: Use this in a service center that needs searchable records from customer calls.

feedback.intrinsic: The game would have no generated character voice.
feedback.instructional: Recognition creates written call records; synthesis creates spoken media.

options.rationale: Live captions are written output from ongoing speech. A game character voice is spoken audio output.
options.better_fit: Use this to make a live meeting accessible to people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

feedback.intrinsic: Players would not hear the character’s generated voice.
feedback.instructional: Captions use recognition. Character voices use synthesis.

options.error_type: Confuses generated audio with clinical dictation
options.rationale: A dictated patient note is clinical documentation created from spoken input. It is not an audio asset for a game.
options.better_fit: Use this when clinicians need to capture patient notes in electronic health records.

feedback.intrinsic: The game’s character would remain without a voice.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis creates audio for media; recognition supports dictated notes.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Speech synthesis can create character voices for games and interactive experiences.

exercises.question_text: Which information can speech synthesis announce? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Synthesis can announce reminders as spoken audio.
Correct. Spoken status updates can reach people who cannot look at a screen.
Correct. Mapping and GPS applications can announce navigation instructions.

options.error_type: Confuses spoken alerts with recognition analysis
options.rationale: Caller sentiment is something analyzed from spoken calls. It is not an alert that synthesis announces.
options.better_fit: Use this when analyzing customer calls for sentiment and common issues.

feedback.intrinsic: Important alerts could go unheard while attention is on another task.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis announces information; recognition can analyze what callers say.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Synthesis can announce reminders, updates, and directions when visual attention is unavailable.

exercises.question_text: A combined voice experience uses recognition for spoken input and synthesis for spoken output.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The interaction would be missing either the spoken request or the spoken response.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Two-way voice experiences combine recognition for input with synthesis for output.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Recognition handles what the person says, and synthesis provides the spoken reply or confirmation.

exercises.question_text: Speech synthesis turns a driver's spoken command into written text.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The driver’s command would not be captured as written input for the requested action.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Recognition handles spoken commands; synthesis can speak confirmations, alerts, or directions.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Turning a spoken command into text is recognition. Synthesis produces spoken audio from text.

exercises.question_text: What can speech recognition create from a customer call?

options.rationale: Correct. Speech recognition transcribes spoken calls into written records that people can search.

options.text: An audio version of a web page
options.rationale: This is spoken audio made from written content. Recognition moves in the opposite direction, from speech to text.
options.better_fit: Use this when people need web content read aloud, such as people with visual impairments or people who cannot look at a screen.

feedback.intrinsic: The call would not become a searchable written record.
feedback.instructional: Remember the direction: recognition listens and writes; synthesis reads written content aloud.

options.rationale: Navigation instructions are audio output. A customer call record is written output from spoken input.
options.better_fit: Use this when a driver needs directions without looking at a screen.

feedback.intrinsic: Agents would still lack a written call record to review.
feedback.instructional: Recognition transcribes what was said; synthesis can announce directions.

options.rationale: Narration is spoken audio created from lesson content. Recognition instead captures speech as written text.
options.better_fit: Use this when an educational platform needs narrated lessons without recording studios.

feedback.intrinsic: The spoken call would remain unrecorded in written form.
feedback.instructional: Choose recognition for call transcription and synthesis for narration.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Recognition turns a spoken customer call into searchable written text.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The reason to use spoken alerts becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: State the capability and action first, then the situation where screens cannot be used.

exercises.correct_answer: Speech synthesis announces alerts when users cannot look at screens
exercises.explanation: The order connects spoken alerts to the reason they matter: visual attention is unavailable. This can improve safety and responsiveness for time-sensitive information.

feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Output, narration, and alerts are spoken results. Recognition handles spoken input.

exercises.explanation: Recognition listens to a person’s words and converts them to text, so it handles the input side of a two-way voice interaction. Synthesis handles the spoken output side.

exercises.question_text: Speech recognition can help route a caller based on what the caller says.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The caller may be sent to the wrong place or wait longer for help.

lessons.title: Choosing speech use cases · Level 2
lessons.slo: Identify when speech recognition, speech synthesis, or both fit a workplace need.

exercises.question_text: Which media items can speech synthesis help create? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Synthesis can help create podcast drafts quickly.
Correct. Synthesis can create audiobook prototypes for rapid development.
Correct. Creators can use synthesis for video and presentation voiceovers.

options.error_type: Confuses media synthesis with meeting recognition
options.rationale: Action-item lists are written meeting documentation. Podcast drafts, audiobooks, and voiceovers are spoken media outputs.
options.better_fit: Use this when meeting conversations need follow-up lists and searchable documentation.

feedback.intrinsic: The media project would not gain the intended audio draft or voiceover.
feedback.instructional: Recognition supports meeting notes and action items. Synthesis creates spoken media.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Synthesis supports podcast drafts, audiobook prototypes, and video voiceovers.

exercises.question_text: What can speech synthesis adjust in a voice-agent response? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Synthesis can adjust tone to shape how a response sounds.
Correct. Synthesis can adjust pace in a spoken response.
Correct. Synthesis can use different speaking styles for more personalized interactions.

options.error_type: Confuses synthesis settings with recognition analysis
options.rationale: Call sentiment is analyzed from what a caller says. Tone, pace, and speaking style describe how the response is spoken.
options.better_fit: Use this when reviewing customer calls to identify sentiment and common issues.

feedback.intrinsic: The response might sound appropriate, but the caller’s sentiment would not be identified.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis shapes output voice qualities. Recognition can analyze spoken calls for sentiment.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Tone, pace, and speaking style all shape a synthesized response.

exercises.question_text: A service center can use speech recognition to create searchable call ___.

parts.text: A service center can use speech recognition to create searchable call

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The service center would not have the written result needed for later search and review.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Audio, alerts, and narration are spoken outputs or source material. Recognition creates searchable call records.

exercises.explanation: Recognition transcribes spoken calls into written records. Those records can be searched for compliance, training, and agent reference.

exercises.question_text: Order the pieces correctly.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: It becomes unclear who is documenting and where the notes belong.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the clinicians, then their dictated notes, then the electronic health records.

exercises.correct_answer: Clinical professionals dictate patient notes into electronic health records
exercises.explanation: The sentence follows the documentation flow: clinicians speak notes, and the notes enter electronic health records. This helps capture details during care.

exercises.question_text: A warehouse worker is carrying boxes and needs to set a reminder without using a screen. Which solution should the team choose?

options.text: A voice assistant that accepts a spoken reminder command
options.rationale: Correct. The worker needs hands-free spoken input to set a reminder while carrying boxes.

options.text: A tool that reads a document aloud
options.error_type: Confuses command input with spoken content output
options.rationale: Reading a document aloud gives spoken output. It does not capture the worker’s reminder command.
options.better_fit: Use this when someone needs to listen to written material instead of reading it.

feedback.intrinsic: The worker still could not set the reminder by speaking.
feedback.instructional: This need starts with a spoken command, so recognition is required.

options.text: A system that narrates a training lesson
options.error_type: Confuses hands-free control with learning narration
options.rationale: Narrated lessons provide educational audio. They do not accept a worker’s request to set a reminder.
options.better_fit: Use this for course content that needs spoken narration.

feedback.intrinsic: The reminder would not be created while the worker carries boxes.
feedback.instructional: Choose a voice assistant when the person must give a hands-free command.

options.text: A tool that creates a game character voice
options.error_type: Confuses workplace command use with media synthesis
options.rationale: A game character voice is media output. It does not support spoken workplace commands.
options.better_fit: Use this for games or interactive media that need character voices.

feedback.intrinsic: The worker’s reminder request would go unhandled.
feedback.instructional: The important need is recognizing the spoken reminder command, not creating media audio.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Recognition lets the assistant receive a spoken reminder request when screens are impractical.

exercises.question_text: During patient appointments, a clinic wants staff to capture details immediately and spend less time typing. Which choices should the clinic use? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dictate notes into electronic health records
options.rationale: Correct. Dictation enters spoken patient notes into electronic health records.
Correct. Clinical professionals can update treatment plans without interrupting care.
Correct. Speaking notes during care helps capture details immediately.

options.error_type: Confuses clinical documentation with media synthesis
options.rationale: Game character voices are media content. They do not document patient care or reduce appointment typing.
options.better_fit: Use this when producing voices for games or interactive experiences.

feedback.intrinsic: Staff would still need another way to capture patient details.
feedback.instructional: This clinic need is spoken documentation, which uses recognition rather than media synthesis.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These choices support spoken clinical documentation and reduce time spent typing.

exercises.question_text: Speech synthesis can read documents ___ for people who cannot read a screen.

parts.text: Speech synthesis can read documents
for people who cannot read a screen.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The person would not receive the document through an audible format.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: “Into text,” captions, and records describe written output. Synthesis reads written documents aloud.

exercises.explanation: Synthesis converts written documents into spoken audio. This provides an audio alternative when reading a screen is difficult or not possible.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The team could take on a complex flow before confirming the most valuable capability.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The recommendation begins with one high-value capability and delays expansion until it is proven.

exercises.correct_answer: Start with one high-value speech capability then expand
exercises.explanation: Begin with the capability that addresses the most valuable need, then prove it works before adding a more complex voice flow. This keeps early work focused.

exercises.question_text: A commuter is driving and wants to consume company articles without reading a screen. Which solution should the company provide?

options.rationale: Correct. The commuter needs written articles converted into spoken audio while driving.
Articles are already written content, so transcription does not meet the need. The commuter needs audio output.
options.better_fit: Use transcription when spoken content needs to become written notes or records.

feedback.intrinsic: The commuter would still have to read rather than listen.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis reads written articles aloud; recognition transcribes spoken words into text.

options.error_type: Confuses content consumption with service recognition
options.rationale: Call routing helps send callers to the right department. It does not make written articles audible.
options.better_fit: Use this in customer service when callers state what they need.

feedback.intrinsic: The commuter would not be able to listen to the articles.
feedback.instructional: Choose synthesis when written content must be heard instead of read.

options.error_type: Confuses spoken output with recognition captions
options.rationale: Live captions turn spoken meetings into written words. The commuter instead needs written articles turned into audio.
options.better_fit: Use this to make a live spoken meeting accessible through written captions.

feedback.intrinsic: The articles would remain silent while the commuter drives.
feedback.instructional: Captions use recognition; reading articles aloud uses synthesis.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Synthesized audio lets the commuter consume written articles without looking at a screen.

exercises.question_text: Educational platforms can use speech synthesis to create narrated ___ without recording studios.

parts.text: Educational platforms can use speech synthesis to create narrated
without recording studios.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Learners would not receive the intended narrated course content.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Call records, captions, and treatment plans are written results of recognition or documentation. Synthesis creates narrated lessons.

exercises.explanation: Synthesis creates spoken course content from written material, so lessons can be narrated without a recording studio. It can also support different learning preferences.

exercises.question_text: A driver says “call home,” and the vehicle must confirm the action aloud. Which design should the vehicle team choose?

options.text: Use speech recognition and speech synthesis together
options.rationale: Correct. Recognition captures “call home” as spoken input, and synthesis provides the audible confirmation.

options.error_type: Confuses two-way interaction with transcription alone
options.rationale: Call transcription can capture the driver’s words as text. It cannot provide the required spoken confirmation.
options.better_fit: Use this when a service center needs searchable written records of customer calls.

feedback.intrinsic: The driver could speak the command but would not hear confirmation.
feedback.instructional: A two-way interaction needs recognition for the command and synthesis for the reply.

options.error_type: Confuses vehicle interaction with learning synthesis
options.rationale: Lesson narration can speak educational content. It does not recognize the driver’s command or make a responsive confirmation.
options.better_fit: Use this when an educational platform needs narrated course material.

feedback.intrinsic: The vehicle would not respond appropriately to “call home.”
feedback.instructional: Narration is one-way audio. The driver needs both spoken input and spoken output.

options.rationale: Navigation alerts provide one-way spoken directions or updates. They do not capture a driver’s command before responding.
options.better_fit: Use this when the vehicle only needs to announce directions or status information.

feedback.intrinsic: The driver’s request would not be received as a command.
feedback.instructional: A confirmation after a spoken request requires recognition plus synthesis.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The vehicle needs recognition for the spoken command and synthesis for the audible confirmation.

exercises.question_text: A factory supervisor must give workers urgent equipment updates while they keep their eyes on machinery. Which features should the factory use? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Spoken status announcements communicate operational information without requiring visual attention.
Correct. Synthesis can deliver urgent information when workers cannot safely look away.
Correct. Spoken updates help workers receive information while focused on machinery.

options.error_type: Confuses alert output with recognition transcription
options.rationale: Transcription creates written text from conversations. The supervisor needs urgent information announced aloud.
options.better_fit: Use this when spoken conversations need written records or captions.

feedback.intrinsic: Workers might not hear the urgent equipment update in time.
feedback.instructional: This need is spoken output for alerts, so use synthesis rather than transcription.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These spoken features deliver urgent information while workers keep visual attention on machinery.

Correct. A person can speak a request to search for information.

options.better_fit: Use this when someone wants to consume written content while driving, exercising, or away from a screen.

options.rationale: A game character script belongs to media creation. It does not store clinical documentation.
options.better_fit: Use this when creating spoken character voices for a game.

exercises.question_text: Which information can speech synthesis announce? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Synthesis can announce reminders as spoken audio.

options.error_type: Confuses spoken alerts with recognition analysis

feedback.intrinsic: Important alerts could go unheard while attention is on another task.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis announces information; recognition can analyze what callers say.

exercises.question_text: A combined voice experience uses recognition for spoken input and synthesis for spoken output.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The interaction would be missing either the spoken request or the spoken response.

exercises.question_text: Which results can meeting transcription create? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Recognition can create written meeting notes that people can search.
Correct. Transcribed conversations can support action-item lists for follow-up.
Correct. Recognition can provide captions while people are speaking.
Navigation directions are spoken audio output. Meeting transcription produces written notes, lists, or captions.
options.better_fit: Use this when drivers need spoken directions without visual attention.

feedback.instructional: Recognition turns meeting speech into text; synthesis can announce navigation directions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The accessibility benefit is hard to understand in the mixed-up sentence.

exercises.correct_answer: Speech synthesis reads web content aloud for people with visual impairments

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The workplace need for hands-free control is unclear.

exercises.question_text: Speech recognition can provide real-time ___ for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

parts.text: Speech recognition can provide real-time
for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A participant could miss spoken parts of the conversation.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Voiceovers, directions, and podcast drafts are audio outputs. Recognition provides live captions from speech.

exercises.question_text: What can synthesized narration provide in language learning?

options.rationale: Correct. Educational platforms can use synthesized speech to provide pronunciation examples.

options.error_type: Confuses learning audio with call transcription
options.rationale: Call records are written transcriptions of spoken customer calls. Pronunciation examples are audio created for learners.
options.better_fit: Use this in service centers that need searchable customer-call documentation.

feedback.intrinsic: Learners would not hear how the words are pronounced.

options.rationale: Caller routing uses spoken requests to direct a call. It does not provide audio for language learning.
