exercises.explanation: A Foundry project is the workspace for Foundry capabilities and client connections. It is the starting place after obtaining an Azure subscription.

exercises.question_text: A mobile app designer needs AI features in a lightweight phone app. Which choices fit this decision? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is correct. An SLM can be a good fit for a lightweight phone application.

options.text: Match the model to the app's needs.
options.rationale: This is correct. Model selection starts with the workload and its constraints.

options.text: Assume a domain-specialized model is required.
options.error_type: Confuses a phone app with a government domain need
options.rationale: A lightweight phone app can be a good SLM use case. Domain specialization is associated with a specialized government application.
options.better_fit: Consider a domain-specialized model for a specialized government workload.

feedback.intrinsic: The designer may add specialization that the lightweight app does not need.
feedback.instructional: Do not assume one model type fits every workload. Start with the app's actual needs.

options.text: Choose a catalog instead of a model.
options.error_type: Confuses a discovery hub with a model choice
options.rationale: The catalog is used to discover and compare models. It is not itself the model selected for the app.
options.better_fit: Use the catalog to locate and compare candidate models.

feedback.intrinsic: The app would still lack a selected model to provide its features.
feedback.instructional: Use the catalog during selection, then choose a model that fits the app.

exercises.explanation: Correct! An SLM is a reasonable choice to consider for a lightweight phone application.

exercises.question_text: Order the pieces correctly.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The catalog's role is no longer communicated clearly.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the catalog, state that it is a central hub, then give its purpose.

exercises.correct_answer: The model catalog is a central hub for discovering and using generative AI models
exercises.explanation: The order identifies the catalog first, then explains its discovery purpose. A catalog brings model choices together so they can be found and compared.

exercises.question_text: Mia has an Azure subscription and needs to deploy a customer-support model in Foundry. What should she create first?

options.rationale: This is correct. Using Foundry capabilities begins by creating a Foundry project.

options.error_type: Confuses comparison information with a workspace
options.rationale: A leaderboard ranks models by attributes such as quality, safety, and throughput. It is not the workspace that begins Foundry work.
options.better_fit: Use a leaderboard when comparing candidate models.

feedback.intrinsic: Mia could compare models but would not have the project needed to proceed.
feedback.instructional: A leaderboard supports selection; a Foundry project is the required starting workspace.

options.error_type: Confuses model behavior settings with project setup
options.rationale: Instructions define a model's role, behavior, style, and constraints. They are configured after the workspace is available.
options.better_fit: Write instructions when defining desired model or agent behavior.

feedback.intrinsic: Mia would define behavior before creating the workspace for the deployment.
feedback.instructional: Start with a Foundry project. Instructions shape behavior but do not establish the project.

options.error_type: Confuses evaluation data with project setup
options.rationale: Benchmarks show performance on standard datasets. They do not replace the project needed to use Foundry capabilities.
options.better_fit: Use benchmark information to compare candidate models.

feedback.intrinsic: Evaluation information alone would not create a place to deploy the model.
feedback.instructional: A Foundry project is the workspace needed first; benchmarks help with model evaluation.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Her Azure subscription lets her begin by creating a Foundry project.

exercises.question_text: A developer is choosing a model for a code-generation feature and sees many catalog choices. What can the developer do in the Foundry model catalog? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is correct. Capabilities are available catalog filters.
This is correct. Inference tasks can be used to narrow choices.
This is correct. Foundry helps users understand and compare model capabilities.

options.text: Use the catalog as an agent tool.
options.error_type: Confuses model discovery with an agent action tool
options.rationale: The catalog is for discovering, filtering, and comparing models. It is not presented as an action an agent can call.
options.better_fit: Use catalog features when selecting a model before deployment.

feedback.intrinsic: The developer would confuse a selection hub with an action-taking capability.
feedback.instructional: Use the catalog to explore models. Agents can call external actions such as APIs, functions, retrieval, or an MCP server.

exercises.explanation: Correct! The catalog supports filtering and comparing models to find a suitable choice.

lessons.title: Models and the Foundry catalog · Level 3
lessons.slo: Describe language models and use the Foundry catalog to find suitable models.

exercises.question_text: What is Microsoft Foundry?

options.text: An environment for generative AI models
options.rationale: This is correct. Foundry supports discovering, evaluating, deploying, and operating generative models.

options.error_type: Confuses the platform with a model
options.rationale: Foundry contains a catalog and deployment options for many models. It is not one model.
options.better_fit: Choose a single model when you need response generation for an application.

feedback.intrinsic: This would mistake the work environment for one of the models used within it.
feedback.instructional: Foundry brings together capabilities for working with many generative models.

options.error_type: Confuses the platform with an evaluation result
options.rationale: Comparison scores help evaluate models. Foundry is the integrated environment where evaluation can occur.
options.better_fit: Use a comparison score when judging model performance.

feedback.intrinsic: A score would not provide the broader workspace for model work.
feedback.instructional: Foundry is an environment; benchmark and comparison results are pieces of evaluation information.

options.error_type: Confuses the platform with a testing feature
options.rationale: Playground settings configure how a deployed model responds. Foundry includes the playground but is broader than it.
options.better_fit: Use playground settings when testing prompts and response behavior.

feedback.intrinsic: This would reduce the full environment to one testing feature.
feedback.instructional: Foundry includes discovery, evaluation, deployment, and operation, not just playground settings.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Foundry is an integrated environment for the model lifecycle.

exercises.question_text: What can a Foundry model entry include? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is correct. A model entry can include benchmark results and performance comparisons.
This is correct. Model entries can list supported fine-tuning options.
This is correct. Entries can include model cards, constraints, and caveats.

options.error_type: Confuses model entry details with an agent capability
options.rationale: An agent can break goals into structured steps and execute workflows. A model entry lists information about the model instead.
options.better_fit: Use an agent when a reusable component must carry out a workflow.

feedback.intrinsic: This would look for a completed worker process where model details should be reviewed.
feedback.instructional: Model entries provide capabilities, benchmarks, tasks, fine-tuning options, and responsible-use documentation.

exercises.explanation: Correct! These details help compare a model's fit, performance, and constraints.

exercises.question_text: Language models are built on top of agents.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: This reverses the relationship between the two.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Language models provide the basis, while agents package a model with instructions and optional actions.

exercises.explanation: Correct! The relationship goes in the other direction: agents are built with models.

exercises.question_text: You can use Microsoft Foundry without an Azure subscription.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The setup would be missing a required starting condition.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use of Foundry requires an Azure subscription, then a Foundry project is created to begin.

exercises.explanation: Correct! An Azure subscription is required to use Foundry.

exercises.question_text: An ___ is the work a model performs when generating or processing output.

parts.text: An
is the work a model performs when generating or processing output.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The selected term would describe measurement, customization, documentation, or scoring rather than output-related work.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use inference task for the work a model performs when generating or processing output. A benchmark result compares performance, fine-tuning adapts a model, model cards document it, and evaluators score outputs.

exercises.explanation: An inference task describes the work performed when a model generates or processes output. Benchmarks, fine-tuning, model cards, and evaluators describe different kinds of information or activities.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The description of the model capability becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with language models, then state their response-generating capability and its generative-AI context.

exercises.correct_answer: Language models generate varied responses for generative AI solutions
exercises.explanation: This sentence focuses on the response variety that language models can support in generative AI solutions.

exercises.question_text: Models sold directly by Azure provide enterprise service level agreements, also called ___.

parts.text: Models sold directly by Azure provide enterprise service level agreements, also called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The chosen term would refer to model size, documentation, or customization instead of a service agreement.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use SLA for service level agreement. LLM and SLM name model types, model cards are documentation, and fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model.

exercises.explanation: SLA means service level agreement. Enterprise-grade SLAs are one benefit of models sold directly by Azure.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The workload-to-model relationship becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Name the government workload first, then connect it to the possible need for a domain-specialized model.

exercises.correct_answer: Government workloads may require a domain-specialized model instead
exercises.explanation: This sentence distinguishes specialized government workloads from lightweight phone-app use cases. Such workloads may need a domain-specialized model.

exercises.question_text: Which filters can you use in the Foundry model catalog? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is correct. The catalog can filter models by source.
This is correct. Capabilities are one available catalog filter.
This is correct. The catalog can filter by inference tasks.

options.error_type: Confuses catalog filtering with an agent capability
options.rationale: Working memory is something agents can maintain during a conversation. It is not listed as a catalog filter.
options.better_fit: Consider working memory when describing what an agent can do in a conversation.

feedback.intrinsic: This would search for an agent behavior instead of narrowing model choices.
feedback.instructional: Catalog filters include source, capabilities, and inference tasks; working memory belongs to agents.

exercises.explanation: Correct! These filters help narrow a large set of model choices.

exercises.question_text: A research lead needs rapid experimentation with an open-source model for a specialized task. Which model source is the best fit?

options.rationale: This is correct. These models include open-source or vendor-hosted choices and support experimentation and specialized tasks.

options.error_type: Confuses enterprise Azure hosting with open-source experimentation
options.rationale: Azure-direct models focus on Microsoft hosting, strong Azure integration, SLAs, security, and compliance. The scenario instead calls for open-source experimentation.
options.better_fit: Choose Azure-direct models when their enterprise Azure features are the priority.

feedback.intrinsic: The research lead could overlook the source type suited to open-source experimentation.
feedback.instructional: Partner and community models are the catalog source associated with open-source choices and rapid innovation.

options.error_type: Confuses general pretrained capability with the model source choice
options.rationale: Foundation models are broad pretrained models that provide general capabilities. This does not identify the source suited to open-source experimentation.
options.better_fit: Use foundation model when describing a pretrained base layer for applications.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead would have a category label but not the needed source choice.
feedback.instructional: The scenario asks about provider and hosting source. Partner and community models fit that need.

options.error_type: Confuses task specialization with provider and hosting source
options.rationale: A specialized task may affect model selection, but this label does not establish an open-source source. Partner and community models include models suitable for specialized tasks.
options.better_fit: Use a domain-specific model when an industry-specific application needs it.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead could focus only on specialization and miss the open-source requirement.
feedback.instructional: Consider both needs: partner and community models support open-source experimentation and specialized work.

exercises.explanation: Correct! Partner and community models are the best match for open-source experimentation on a specialized task.

exercises.question_text: The Foundry model catalog is a central hub for models from many providers.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: This would overlook why the catalog is useful for comparing choices.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The catalog is a central hub for discovering and using models from an extensive range of providers.

exercises.explanation: Correct! The catalog brings together a wide selection of models from many providers.

exercises.question_text: A government service lead is selecting AI for a specialized public-service workload. Which considerations best support the choice? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is correct. A government application may require a domain-specialized model.

options.text: Match the model to the workload.
options.rationale: This is correct. Different workloads can require different model types.

options.text: Choose an SLM because it suits phone apps.
options.error_type: Confuses the lightweight phone-app use case with a specialized government workload
options.rationale: An SLM may suit a lightweight phone app. That does not make it the stated choice for specialized government work.
options.better_fit: Consider an SLM when a lightweight phone application is the workload.

feedback.intrinsic: The service could select based on an unrelated mobile-app situation.
feedback.instructional: Choose based on the actual workload. Specialized government work may need a domain-specialized model.

options.text: Use a foundation-model label as the selection rule.
options.error_type: Confuses a model category with a workload-based decision
options.rationale: A foundation model is a broad pretrained model category. The selection should still consider workload and task needs.
options.better_fit: Use the foundation-model category when describing general pretrained models.

feedback.intrinsic: A broad label alone would not show whether the model fits the public-service workload.
feedback.instructional: Model categories are useful descriptions, but fit comes from matching the model to the workload.

exercises.explanation: Correct! A specialized government workload may call for a domain-specialized model, selected to fit the work.

lessons.title: Choose and evaluate models · Level 1
lessons.slo: Choose a model approach for a task and explain how Foundry evaluates models.

exercises.question_text: Which task-to-model matches are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: text-embedding-3-small is an embedding model. Embedding models are built for semantic vector representations.
GPT-5.1-codex is listed as a recommended model type for coding. It supports the coding task category.
Phi-4-multimodal-instruct is listed for multimodal work. Multimodal chat can include images, audio, and video.

options.error_type: Confuses chat model with embedding model
options.rationale: GPT-4.1 is optimized for real-time chat and customer support. Embeddings require an embedding model such as text-embedding-3-small.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-4.1 for fast interactive chat at scale.

feedback.intrinsic: Search by meaning would not be matched to the model type built for semantic vectors.
feedback.instructional: Task type matters. Use embedding models for semantic vector representations and GPT-4.1 for real-time chat.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Each selected pairing matches the model type to the task it is recommended for.

exercises.question_text: Which model is described as an Anthropic frontier-level model?

options.rationale: Claude Opus 4.5 is described as an Anthropic frontier-level model. It is intended for sophisticated agents and difficult reasoning tasks.
GPT-5.x is optimized for reasoning, planning, and agentic workflows. It is not the Anthropic model named here.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-5.x for structured logic, multi-step reasoning, and adjustable thinking levels.

feedback.intrinsic: A team needing the stated Anthropic option would begin evaluating the wrong family.
feedback.instructional: Keep the model names distinct: Claude Opus 4.5 is the Anthropic frontier-level choice.

options.error_type: Confuses general-purpose model with frontier agent model
options.rationale: Mistral Large 3 is a general-purpose model that balances quality, throughput, cost, and latency. It is not described as Anthropic’s frontier-level model.
options.better_fit: Choose Mistral Large 3 for balanced multilingual drafting or business-report work.

feedback.intrinsic: The selection would emphasize balance rather than the specified frontier-level capability.
feedback.instructional: Mistral Large 3 is a different model with a different focus. The Anthropic frontier-level model is Claude Opus 4.5.

options.error_type: Confuses real-time chat model with frontier model
options.rationale: GPT-4.1 is optimized for responsive, high-volume chat. It is not the Anthropic frontier-level model.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-4.1 for real-time chat, customer support, and interactive applications.

feedback.intrinsic: The choice would favor fast scale instead of the requested sophisticated-agent work.
feedback.instructional: GPT-4.1 and Claude Opus 4.5 solve different needs. The latter is the frontier-level Anthropic option.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Claude Opus 4.5 is the Anthropic frontier-level model in this set.

exercises.question_text: Text-embedding-3-small is built mainly for generating chat replies.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A search-by-meaning feature could be designed around the wrong task type.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Embedding models represent meaning as vectors. Use chat models when the main task is generating conversational replies.

exercises.explanation: Correct. text-embedding-3-small is built for semantic vector representations, not primarily chat replies.

exercises.question_text: Claude Opus 4.5 can suit complex code reasoning and multi-step computer-use tasks.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That choice could steer a long, complex task toward a model selected for a different strength.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Claude Opus 4.5 is suited to sophisticated agents, difficult code reasoning, and multi-step computer-use tasks.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Complex code reasoning and multi-step computer use are stated strengths of Claude Opus 4.5.

exercises.question_text: Which uses fit Mistral Large 3? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Mistral Large 3 is suitable for multilingual drafting. This is one of its stated general-purpose uses.
Mistral Large 3 can support structured business report generation. This fits its balance of quality and efficient throughput.
Mistral Large 3 can fit mid-latency agent tasks. It is positioned for balanced cost and performance.

options.error_type: Confuses Mistral Large 3 with GPT-4.1 focus
options.rationale: Mistral Large 3 has broader general-purpose uses than customer chat alone. Real-time customer support is a stated strength of GPT-4.1.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-4.1 for real-time chat and high-volume customer support.

feedback.intrinsic: A team could unnecessarily limit a balanced general-purpose model to one narrow workload.
feedback.instructional: Mistral Large 3 supports several kinds of work. GPT-4.1 is the model optimized for speedy support chat.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These are stated uses for Mistral Large 3’s balanced general-purpose capabilities.

exercises.question_text: What is a model family?

options.rationale: A model family contains related models that share architecture or lineage. Members can still differ in size, capability, specialization, or version.
An endpoint is created when a configured model is deployed. It is not a group of related models.
options.better_fit: Use this phrase when describing how an application calls a deployed model.

feedback.intrinsic: This would make it harder to compare related model choices before deployment.
feedback.instructional: Separate the group from the deployment: a family is related models, while deployment makes one configured model available.

options.text: A group sold directly by Azure
options.rationale: Models sold directly by Azure are one catalog source. A family is defined by shared lineage, not by who sells it.
options.better_fit: Use this when comparing Azure-sold models with partner or community models.

feedback.intrinsic: You could overlook related models that come from a different catalog source.
feedback.instructional: Provider source and model lineage answer different questions. A family describes related architecture or history.

options.error_type: Confuses a family with model input
options.rationale: A prompt is input sent to a model. It is not a collection of related models.
options.better_fit: Use this when describing a request sent to a model.

feedback.intrinsic: You would be naming the request instead of the group of models.
feedback.instructional: Remember that a family groups models; a prompt supplies input to one model.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A family groups related models, even when members differ in size or capability.

exercises.question_text: Mistral Large 3 is designed only for high-volume, low-latency production chat.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That choice could restrict a model’s use to fast chat even when multilingual drafting or business reports are needed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The high-volume, low-latency focus describes GPT-4.1. Mistral Large 3 is broader and balances several trade-offs.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Mistral Large 3 is a general-purpose model that balances quality, throughput, cost, and latency.

exercises.question_text: Foundation models are large pretrained models that can provide general capabilities out of the box.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That choice would rule out a ready-to-deploy base model for a general task.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Foundation models are large pretrained models. They can be deployed immediately or customized through fine-tuning.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Foundation models already provide general language, reasoning, or multimodal capabilities.

exercises.question_text: Which model is available to all Foundry users?

options.rationale: GPT-4.1 is stated as available to all Foundry users. It is also optimized for responsive chat at scale.
GPT-5 model-family availability is currently restricted by registration. It is not the all-user option.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-5.x when registration is available and multi-step reasoning or planning is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: A team could plan for a model family before confirming that registration is complete.
feedback.instructional: Availability matters during selection. GPT-4.1 is available to all Foundry users, while GPT-5.x requires registration.

options.error_type: Confuses Anthropic model with Foundry availability note
options.rationale: Claude Opus 4.5 is identified for frontier-level complex work. The all-user availability statement applies to GPT-4.1.
options.better_fit: Choose Claude Opus 4.5 for long-context complex code reasoning or computer-use tasks.

feedback.intrinsic: The team might mistake a capability description for the specific availability note.
feedback.instructional: Keep availability separate from capability. GPT-4.1 is the model explicitly available to all Foundry users.

options.error_type: Confuses catalog availability with all-user availability
options.rationale: Mistral Large 3 is a balanced general-purpose catalog model. The all-user availability statement names GPT-4.1 instead.
options.better_fit: Choose Mistral Large 3 for multilingual drafting or balanced quality, cost, and latency.

feedback.intrinsic: The team could confuse being in the catalog with the stated all-user access detail.
feedback.instructional: Catalog presence and the all-user availability note are different. The noted model is GPT-4.1.

exercises.explanation: Correct. GPT-4.1 is the model explicitly available to all Foundry users.

exercises.question_text: Which are strengths of GPT-5.x? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: GPT-5.x is optimized for multi-step reasoning. This supports work that needs several connected reasoning steps.
Structured logic and planning are stated strengths of GPT-5.x. These strengths suit complex, organized work.
GPT-5.x supports adjustable thinking levels. They let developers trade speed for accuracy.
This is the main optimization of GPT-4.1. GPT-5.x is described for reasoning, logic, planning, and agentic workflows.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-4.1 for real-time chat and high-volume production workloads.

feedback.intrinsic: Choosing for this reason could slow a busy customer-support experience.
feedback.instructional: Match GPT-5.x to reasoning-heavy work. Match GPT-4.1 to speed, efficiency, and low-latency scale.

exercises.explanation: Correct. GPT-5.x combines reasoning, planning, and adjustable thinking levels.

exercises.question_text: GPT-4.1 is optimized for speed, efficiency, and low-latency inference.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A fast interactive workload could be matched to a model chosen for deeper reasoning instead.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: GPT-4.1 is optimized for speed, efficiency, and low-latency inference, especially at production scale.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These strengths make GPT-4.1 suitable for responsive, high-volume applications.

exercises.question_text: GPT-5.x is available to all Foundry users without registration.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A team could plan around a model family before confirming that it is available to them.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: GPT-5.x currently requires registration. GPT-4.1 is the model stated as available to all Foundry users.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Registration currently restricts access to the GPT-5 model family.

flashcards.back: Related models sharing lineage but differing in size, capability, specialization, or version.
For multi-step reasoning, planning, and agentic workflows.
For complex agents, code reasoning, and long-context tasks.
Real-time, high-volume chat with speed and low latency.

lessons.title: Choose and evaluate models · Level 2
lessons.slo: Choose a model approach for a task and explain how Foundry evaluates models.

exercises.question_text: Domain-tuned catalog models can fit industry-specific applications such as finance, healthcare, or legal work.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A specialized business need could be treated as if every general model were equally targeted to that domain.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: For finance, healthcare, or legal applications, the catalog can provide domain-tuned model options.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Domain-tuned catalog models are recommended for industry-specific applications.

exercises.question_text: For high-volume production workloads that need fast responses, choose ___.

parts.text: For high-volume production workloads that need fast responses, choose

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The workload could be assigned to a model selected for deep reasoning, balanced general use, or complex long-context work instead of speed at scale.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use GPT-4.1 for the speed-and-scale clue. GPT-5.x emphasizes reasoning, Mistral balances trade-offs, and Claude Opus 4.5 fits complex long-context tasks.

exercises.explanation: GPT-4.1 is optimized for speed, efficiency, and low-latency inference. It is better suited than reasoning-heavy models for high-volume production workloads.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The trade-off would be unclear to a teammate reading the statement.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Place the model first, then its feature, then the purpose of that feature: trading speed for accuracy.

exercises.correct_answer: GPT-5.x supports thinking levels to trade speed for accuracy
exercises.explanation: The sentence links GPT-5.x to adjustable thinking levels and then states their purpose. Those levels let a developer favor speed or accuracy as needed.

exercises.question_text: A customer-support manager needs a virtual agent to answer many customer questions quickly, day and night. Which model fits best?

options.rationale: GPT-4.1 is optimized for real-time chat and customer support. Its speed and low latency suit many customer questions.

options.error_type: Confuses reasoning focus with low-latency scale
options.rationale: GPT-5.x is optimized for multi-step reasoning, planning, and agentic workflows. The manager’s priority is rapid, high-volume support.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-5.x for structured logic, planning, or accuracy-focused multi-step work.

feedback.intrinsic: Customers may wait longer than necessary when the key need is fast support at scale.
feedback.instructional: Choose for the main workload. GPT-4.1 is optimized for responsive customer-support chat.

options.error_type: Confuses complex agent work with real-time support
options.rationale: Claude Opus 4.5 is suited to sophisticated agents, complex code reasoning, and computer-use tasks. The scenario does not require those specialized strengths.
options.better_fit: Choose Claude Opus 4.5 for long specifications, complex code reasoning, or multi-step computer use.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager could select for complex work while neglecting the high-volume speed requirement.
feedback.instructional: Fast customer support points to GPT-4.1. Reserve Claude Opus 4.5 for its stated complex-agent strengths.

options.error_type: Confuses balanced general use with optimized low latency
options.rationale: Mistral Large 3 balances quality, throughput, cost, and latency. GPT-4.1 is specifically optimized for real-time, high-volume support.
options.better_fit: Choose Mistral Large 3 for balanced multilingual drafting, reports, or mid-latency tasks.

feedback.intrinsic: The service might receive a balanced option when the central need is the fastest scalable chat.
feedback.instructional: Balanced performance is different from an explicit low-latency focus. GPT-4.1 is the stronger fit here.

exercises.explanation: Correct. GPT-4.1 is optimized for fast, high-volume real-time chat and customer support.

exercises.question_text: For long specifications and multi-file diffs, use ___ when its large context window is useful.

parts.text: For long specifications and multi-file diffs, use
when its large context window is useful.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A long specification could be matched to a model whose stated focus is speed, balance, or different reasoning needs.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use Claude Opus 4.5 for the large-context clue. GPT-5.x emphasizes reasoning and planning, Mistral balances trade-offs, and GPT-4.1 emphasizes low latency.

exercises.explanation: Claude Opus 4.5 has large context and output windows. That makes it useful when a task includes long specifications or changes across several files.

exercises.question_text: A developer is building a technical-report assistant. The reports require several reasoning steps, and the developer can favor accuracy over speed. Which GPT-5.x choices fit? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: GPT-5.x is optimized for structured logic. That matches reports requiring connected reasoning steps.
Adjustable thinking levels let developers trade speed for accuracy. The scenario explicitly favors accuracy.
GPT-5.x is optimized for agentic workflows. It can fit a report assistant that handles structured work.

options.text: Choose it for fastest chat at scale
options.rationale: Fast, high-volume chat is the stated fit for GPT-4.1. The report scenario instead emphasizes reasoning and accuracy.
options.better_fit: Choose GPT-4.1 when rapid responses at scale are the main need.

feedback.intrinsic: This would focus the choice on speed when the report needs careful reasoning.

lessons.title: Compare, score, and deploy models · Level 1
lessons.slo: Evaluate model outputs and explain what happens when a model is deployed.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe benchmark results? Select all that apply.

options.text: They show performance on standard datasets.
options.rationale: Benchmark results report performance using standard datasets. Shared datasets support consistent comparisons.

options.text: They make model comparison more consistent.
options.rationale: Common evaluation data gives comparisons a consistent basis. This helps compare candidate models.
Benchmarks provide performance evidence. They do not alter or repair responses.
options.better_fit: Use benchmark results to identify performance strengths and weaknesses.

options.rationale: Endpoints are created through deployment. Benchmarking occurs during evaluation.
options.better_fit: Use deployment to make a model available through an API endpoint.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Benchmarks provide consistent performance evidence.

exercises.question_text: What does a model leaderboard do?

options.rationale: A leaderboard ranks models by attributes such as quality, safety, and throughput. It helps identify candidates.
Own-data prompt testing belongs to the benchmark flow. A leaderboard ranks models.
options.better_fit: Use Try with your own data to test prompts.

options.rationale: Groundedness is an AI-assisted output-quality metric. It is not the purpose of a leaderboard.
options.better_fit: Use groundedness to judge whether an output is supported by material.

options.rationale: Safety evaluators scan outputs for harms. A leaderboard ranks models instead.
options.better_fit: Use a safety evaluator to scan output safety.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Leaderboards rank models by attributes.

exercises.question_text: Benchmark scores help compare models by using consistent evaluation criteria.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Comparable scores could be misunderstood as unrelated evidence.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Benchmark results use standard datasets to make comparison more consistent.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Consistent criteria make scores comparable.

exercises.question_text: Side-by-side model comparison cannot include cost as a comparison attribute.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: An important procurement criterion would be excluded unnecessarily.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Side-by-side comparison supports cost along with other selection attributes.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Cost can be compared with quality, security, compliance, and performance.

exercises.question_text: What is the prebuilt option for a well-defined use case?

options.rationale: A Foundry tool is a prebuilt option for a clearly defined use case. It can provide predictable performance and built-in compliance.
A leaderboard ranks candidate models by attributes. It does not provide a prebuilt task solution.
options.better_fit: Use a leaderboard when ranking models by quality, safety, or throughput.

options.rationale: A safety evaluator scans outputs for harms. It does not provide the requested task capability.
options.better_fit: Use a safety evaluator to scan generated outputs for safety concerns.

options.rationale: Comparison weighs attributes across models. It does not replace selection with a prebuilt solution.
options.better_fit: Use comparison when evaluating trade-offs between model candidates.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A Foundry tool is the prebuilt option.

exercises.question_text: Which are classic NLP metrics? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Accuracy is a classic NLP metric. It is part of traditional metric-based scoring.
Precision is a classic NLP metric. It belongs to traditional NLP evaluation.
Recall is a classic NLP metric. It is commonly grouped with accuracy, precision, and F1.
Groundedness is an AI-assisted quality metric. It supports qualitative scoring beyond traditional measures.
options.better_fit: Use groundedness to assess whether output is supported by provided information.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Accuracy, precision, and recall are classic NLP metrics.

exercises.question_text: A Foundry tool requires custom model building before it can be used.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Custom-model work would delay the solution.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Foundry tools provide fast time-to-value without custom modeling.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Foundry tools use prebuilt models.

exercises.question_text: AI-assisted metrics can provide qualitative scoring beyond traditional NLP metrics.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Qualitative output concerns could be missed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Groundedness, relevance, coherence and fluency, and GPT similarity support qualitative scoring.

exercises.explanation: Correct. AI-assisted metrics support qualitative judgments.

exercises.question_text: Which events occur during model deployment? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Deployment allocates CPUs, GPUs, memory, networking, and scaling rules. These resources run the model.

options.text: A secure API endpoint is created.
options.rationale: Deployment creates a secure endpoint for application calls. This enables production access.
Deployment activates monitoring and logging for operational information. This includes usage, latency, errors, and costs.
Deployment does not repair evaluation results. It prepares a model for production operation.
options.better_fit: Use benchmark results to inspect performance evidence.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Deployment allocates resources, creates an endpoint, and activates monitoring.

exercises.question_text: What do Foundry evaluators measure?

options.rationale: Foundry evaluators measure quality, safety, and effectiveness of model or agent outputs. The Evaluator Library provides reusable evaluators.
Token limits concern deployment capacity. Evaluators assess outputs.
options.better_fit: Use capacity settings when configuring deployment throughput.

options.rationale: System instructions guide behavior before output generation. Evaluators measure resulting outputs.
options.better_fit: Use a system instruction to define behavior and guardrails.

options.rationale: Catalog filters narrow model choices. Evaluators score outputs.
options.better_fit: Use catalog filters when discovering models.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Evaluators measure output quality, safety, and effectiveness.

exercises.question_text: Deploying a model activates monitoring and logging for usage, latency, errors, and costs.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Important production signals could be omitted from planning.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Deployment activates monitoring and logging for usage, performance, latency, errors, and costs.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Deployment activates operational monitoring and logging.

exercises.question_text: A safety evaluator automatically resolves harmful content after detecting it.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Detected harmful content could remain unaddressed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A safety evaluator identifies harms; remediation requires a separate response.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Safety evaluators detect, scan, and score issues rather than resolving them.

flashcards.back: A prebuilt model solution for a well-defined use case.
Scores showing model performance on standard datasets.
It ranks models by attributes such as quality and safety.
Making a model available through a secure production endpoint.

exercises.question_text: A developer selected a support model and needs to test it with real support prompts before deployment. Which actions should the developer take? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Benchmarks is part of the practical evaluation flow. It is the starting area for own-data testing.

feedback.intrinsic: The model could be available without safety review.

exercises.question_text: A model ___ ranks models by quality, safety, and throughput.

ranks models by quality, safety, and throughput.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That term names a different evaluation or discovery feature.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The technical term is leaderboard.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the sentence about a quality metric.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The metric's purpose would not be expressed clearly.

exercises.correct_answer: Use relevance to assess answer fit to the request

exercises.question_text: A procurement manager must choose between two models and weigh cost, security, and performance. What should the manager use?

options.rationale: Side-by-side comparison weighs selection attributes across candidate models. The listed criteria are supported comparison dimensions.

feedback.instructional: The manager needs a comparison feature, not an instruction.

exercises.question_text: A reviewer is assessing AI-generated study guides for support by source material, fit to the question, and readable writing. Which metrics should the reviewer select? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Groundedness assesses whether output is supported by provided material. It fits the source-support need.
Relevance assesses whether an answer fits the request. It fits the question-alignment need.
Coherence and fluency assess readability and logical flow. They fit the writing-quality need.
Tokens per minute concerns deployment capacity. It does not assess qualitative answer quality.
options.better_fit: Use tokens per minute when allocating deployment capacity.

feedback.intrinsic: The reviewer would learn about throughput rather than quality.
feedback.instructional: Use the AI-assisted metrics that match support, relevance, and writing quality.

lessons.title: Compare, score, and deploy models · Level 3
lessons.slo: Evaluate model outputs and explain what happens when a model is deployed.

exercises.question_text: Which events occur during model deployment? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Deployment allocates CPUs, GPUs, memory, networking, and scaling rules. These resources run the model.

options.text: A secure API endpoint is created.
options.rationale: Deployment creates a secure endpoint for application calls. This enables production access.
Deployment activates monitoring and logging for operational information. This includes usage, latency, errors, and costs.
Deployment does not repair evaluation results. It prepares a model for production operation.
options.better_fit: Use benchmark results to inspect performance evidence.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Deployment allocates resources, creates an endpoint, and activates monitoring.

exercises.question_text: What do benchmark results measure model performance on?

options.rationale: Benchmark results use standard datasets to measure performance. This supports consistent comparisons.
Production logs track deployed operation. They are not the shared datasets used by benchmarks.
options.better_fit: Use monitoring logs to inspect deployed usage, latency, errors, and costs.

options.rationale: Safety settings are deployment configuration. They are not benchmark evaluation data.
options.better_fit: Use safety settings when configuring safeguards for deployment.

options.rationale: API endpoints let applications call deployed models. They do not measure benchmark performance.
options.better_fit: Use an endpoint after deployment to call a model.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Benchmark results use standard datasets.

exercises.question_text: AI-assisted metrics can provide qualitative scoring beyond traditional NLP metrics.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Qualitative output concerns could be missed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Groundedness, relevance, coherence and fluency, and GPT similarity support qualitative scoring.

exercises.explanation: Correct. AI-assisted metrics support qualitative judgments.

exercises.question_text: A safety evaluator automatically resolves harmful content after detecting it.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Detected harmful content could remain unaddressed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A safety evaluator identifies harms; remediation requires a separate response.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Safety evaluators detect, scan, and score issues rather than resolving them.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the filtering statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The selection relationship would be unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: State the filtering action, then the candidates, then the criteria.

exercises.correct_answer: Apply filters to narrow models by industry and licensing

exercises.question_text: A marketing team is choosing metrics for AI-written product descriptions. It needs qualitative evidence of factual support, writing clarity, and similarity to an approved reference style. Which choices best fit? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Groundedness provides qualitative evidence about factual support. It addresses whether claims are supported.
Coherence and fluency assess clarity and flow of writing. They address the writing-quality criterion.
GPT similarity is an AI-assisted quality metric. It fits comparison with an approved reference style.
F1 is a classic NLP metric. By itself it does not provide the requested qualitative evidence.
options.better_fit: Use F1 when a traditional quantitative metric is specifically needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The team would miss the required qualitative review.
feedback.instructional: Use AI-assisted metrics for qualitative qualities beyond F1.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These metrics address the stated quality dimensions.

exercises.question_text: Foundry tools use ___ to provide fast time-to-value without custom modeling.

parts.text: Foundry tools use
to provide fast time-to-value without custom modeling.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That term would describe a different capability.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The key term is prebuilt models.

exercises.explanation: Foundry tools rely on prebuilt models rather than requiring custom model development.

exercises.question_text: A healthcare lead must narrow candidates by industry and licensing, then weigh compliance, quality, and cost. Which approach best supports this decision?

options.rationale: Filters narrow candidates by industry and licensing. Comparison then supports the required trade-offs.
Benchmark scores provide consistent performance evidence. They do not apply the stated industry and licensing filters.
options.better_fit: Use benchmarks when standard-dataset performance is the main need.

feedback.intrinsic: Candidates could fail licensing or industry requirements.
feedback.instructional: Use filters first, then compare the narrowed choices.

options.rationale: AI-assisted metrics qualitatively score outputs. They do not narrow catalog candidates by licensing.
options.better_fit: Use AI-assisted metrics to evaluate output qualities such as relevance.

feedback.intrinsic: The candidate list would remain too broad.
feedback.instructional: This decision needs catalog filters and model comparison.

options.rationale: Unfiltered browsing ignores identified selection requirements. It also lacks a structured trade-off view.
options.better_fit: Browse without filters when no narrowing criteria exist.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead would review unnecessary candidates.
feedback.instructional: Apply the stated filters, then compare attributes directly.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Filtering and comparison match the workflow.

exercises.question_text: A support manager must choose between a catalog model, an agent action, and a prebuilt Foundry capability for a single standardized workflow. Fast time-to-value and built-in compliance matter most. Which decision is best?

options.rationale: The workflow is standardized, and speed and compliance are priorities. A Foundry tool uses prebuilt models for this need.
Catalog selection is useful when choosing among model capabilities. It adds selection work when a prebuilt solution fits.
options.better_fit: Select a catalog model when the use case requires a tailored choice among model capabilities.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager would take on extra selection work.
feedback.instructional: For a fixed workflow, a Foundry tool is the closer fit.

options.rationale: Agent actions let an agent call external capabilities. They are not the prebuilt solution described.
options.better_fit: Use an agent action when an agent must call an API or retrieve external information.

feedback.intrinsic: An action alone would not deliver the standardized solution.
feedback.instructional: This decision concerns a prebuilt Foundry capability, not an agent integration.

options.rationale: A leaderboard helps rank models. It does not provide the requested workflow solution.
options.better_fit: Open a leaderboard when comparing model attributes before selection.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager would have rankings but no direct solution.
feedback.instructional: A Foundry tool is intended for the defined workflow.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The criteria favor a Foundry tool.

exercises.question_text: A ___ scans outputs for harmful or unsafe content.

parts.text: A
scans outputs for harmful or unsafe content.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That term would not name the safety-scanning component.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The required term is safety evaluator.

exercises.explanation: A safety evaluator performs safety scanning on outputs.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the own-data testing flow.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A later testing action would occur before setup.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Follow selection, Benchmarks, own-data, testing, and inspection.

exercises.correct_answer: Choose a model Select Benchmarks Choose own data Test prompts Inspect responses
exercises.explanation: Choose the model and benchmark area before selecting own data. Test prompts before inspecting their responses.

exercises.question_text: What does deployment make available to applications?

options.rationale: Deployment makes the selected model available through a stable, scalable, secure endpoint. Applications usually call it through an API.
A leaderboard ranks models by attributes. It is not an application access point.
options.better_fit: Use a leaderboard before selection to compare models.

options.rationale: Benchmark datasets support performance evaluation. They do not let an application call a model.
options.better_fit: Use benchmark datasets when evaluating performance.

options.rationale: A safety metric assesses output qualities. It does not provide production connectivity.
options.better_fit: Use a safety metric when evaluating output safety.

lessons.title: Deploy and test a model · Level 1
lessons.slo: Configure a deployed model and test it in the Foundry playground.

exercises.question_text: What does temperature control? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Temperature controls creative variation in responses. It balances variation against repeatability.
Temperature also affects response repeatability. It controls the balance between repeatability and variation.
Max output tokens caps response length. Temperature controls variation and repeatability instead.
options.better_fit: Use this when setting a firm response-length cap.

feedback.intrinsic: Replies may vary differently but remain equally long.
feedback.instructional: Use temperature for variation and max output tokens for length.

options.rationale: Role and guardrails come from system instructions. Temperature does not define those rules.
options.better_fit: Use this when setting behavior, tone, tools, or guardrails.

feedback.intrinsic: Variation may change without adding role guidance.
feedback.instructional: Use instructions for behavior and temperature for variation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Temperature balances variation with repeatability.

exercises.question_text: What does deployment type determine?

options.text: Where and how inference is processed
options.rationale: Deployment type determines where and how inference is processed. It is connected to throughput and data-processing requirements.
A model version identifies a particular release. It does not define the processing arrangement.
options.better_fit: Use this when identifying a specific release of a selected model.

feedback.intrinsic: The processing decision would remain unresolved.
feedback.instructional: Use deployment type for inference processing and version for release identity.

options.rationale: Max output tokens caps response length. Deployment type concerns processing instead.
options.better_fit: Use this when setting a firm maximum response length.

feedback.intrinsic: Replies may change length while processing needs remain unmet.
feedback.instructional: Max output tokens controls length; deployment type controls processing.

options.rationale: Temperature controls variation and repeatability. It does not select an inference arrangement.
options.better_fit: Use this when adjusting creativity versus repeatability.

feedback.intrinsic: Reply style may change without resolving deployment requirements.
feedback.instructional: Temperature affects variation; deployment type affects inference processing.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Deployment type determines where and how inference is processed.

exercises.question_text: Temperature controls the balance between creative variation and more repeatable responses.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A length or capacity setting might be changed for a consistency problem.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Temperature affects variation versus repeatability; it does not set length or capacity.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Temperature adjusts that balance.

exercises.question_text: A model version determines where and how inference is processed.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The release label would be mistaken for a processing decision.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Model version identifies the release, while deployment type determines where and how inference runs.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A version identifies a release; deployment type controls processing.

exercises.question_text: Which can a system prompt set? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A system prompt can set the assistant's behavior. It establishes how the assistant should operate.
A system prompt can define tone. Tone guides how responses are expressed.
A system prompt can establish tools and guardrails. These guide capabilities and boundaries.
Max output tokens sets the response-length cap. A system prompt instead sets behavior-related guidance.
options.better_fit: Use this when setting a firm maximum response length.

feedback.intrinsic: Behavior may be specified while replies remain longer than intended.
feedback.instructional: Use max output tokens for length and a system prompt for behavior guidance.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A system prompt can set behavior, tone, tools, and guardrails.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about token and request limits are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: TPM limits token traffic per minute
options.rationale: TPM is an allocation and rate limit for token traffic per minute. It measures token capacity over time.
RPM limits how many requests can be handled per minute. It counts requests rather than tokens.
Temperature controls response variation. RPM controls request count per minute.
options.better_fit: Use temperature when adjusting creativity or repeatability.

feedback.intrinsic: Busy-period request limits would remain unchanged.
feedback.instructional: Use RPM for request count and temperature for variation.

options.rationale: Model version identifies a release. TPM limits token traffic per minute.
options.better_fit: Use model version when selecting a particular release.

feedback.intrinsic: Release identity would be confused with traffic capacity.
feedback.instructional: TPM is the token-traffic limit, not a version label.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TPM concerns token traffic and RPM concerns request count.

exercises.question_text: A user prompt is the end user's request or question.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The user's request could be confused with behavior guidance.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A user prompt states the request; a system prompt guides the assistant's behavior.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A user prompt contains what the end user asks for.

exercises.question_text: What is the Foundry playground?

options.text: A portal interface for deployed models
options.rationale: The playground is a portal interface for interacting with a deployed model. It supports prompt testing and settings capture.
A model catalog is for discovering and comparing models. The playground is for interacting with a deployed model.
options.better_fit: Use this when searching for and comparing available models.

feedback.intrinsic: A developer may search instead of test a deployment.
feedback.instructional: Use the playground for interactive testing and the catalog for discovery.

options.rationale: An API lets application code call a deployment. The playground is an interactive portal interface.
options.better_fit: Use this when implementing programmatic model calls.

feedback.intrinsic: Coding could begin before settings are tested.
feedback.instructional: Use the playground to test first, then use an API in code.

options.rationale: A chat client is an application that sends and displays messages. The playground is the portal testing workspace.
options.better_fit: Use this when describing a small app for model conversations.

feedback.intrinsic: A client could be built before the approach is validated.
feedback.instructional: The playground is for testing a deployed model interactively.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The playground is the portal interface for a deployed model.

exercises.question_text: Higher TPM allocation increases a deployment's capacity for token traffic per minute.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The available capacity would be underestimated.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: TPM is token-traffic capacity per minute; raising it increases capacity.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Higher TPM increases token-traffic capacity.

exercises.question_text: Which effects can max output tokens have? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Max output tokens directly caps response length. This is its primary function.
The setting affects how many output tokens a response can consume. Larger limits can use more token capacity.
High output-token limits can contribute to rate-limit pressure. Therefore the setting can affect throttling behavior.
Instructions set an assistant's role and behavior. Max output tokens concerns response length.
options.better_fit: Use this when defining behavior, tone, tools, or guardrails.

feedback.intrinsic: Replies may become shorter without receiving role guidance.
feedback.instructional: Use instructions for role and max output tokens for length.

exercises.explanation: Correct. This setting affects length, token use, and throttling pressure.

exercises.question_text: The Foundry playground is used only after all application code is written.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The team could build around untested prompts.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use the playground to test prompts, compare models, and capture settings before writing code.

exercises.explanation: Correct. It helps test prompts and settings before coding.

exercises.question_text: Max output tokens sets the assistant's behavior, tone, tools, and guardrails.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A team could adjust length when it intended to define behavior.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use system instructions for behavior, tone, tools, and guardrails; use max output tokens for response length.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Instructions set those elements; max output tokens caps length.

exercises.question_text: A support team must choose where and how its virtual agent's inference will be processed. Which setting should it select?

options.rationale: Deployment type determines where and how inference is processed. That is the decision described in the scenario.
Model version selects a particular release. It does not choose the inference arrangement.
options.better_fit: Use this when a team must select a specific model release.

feedback.intrinsic: A release could be chosen while processing remains undecided.
feedback.instructional: Choose deployment type for processing and model version for release identity.

options.rationale: Temperature controls response variation and repeatability. It does not determine processing location or method.
options.better_fit: Use this when response consistency or creativity must change.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent's style may change without solving the deployment decision.
feedback.instructional: Temperature affects outputs; deployment type affects inference processing.

options.rationale: System instructions set behavior and guardrails. They do not select where inference runs.
options.better_fit: Use this when defining the assistant's role, tone, or rules.

feedback.intrinsic: Behavior may be configured while processing needs remain open.
feedback.instructional: Use instructions for behavior and deployment type for processing.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Deployment type is the processing-arrangement decision.

exercises.question_text: A support manager is configuring a virtual agent. It must answer in concise bullets, identify itself as a support assistant, and refuse diagnosis requests. Which instructions belong in the system prompt? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A system prompt can specify output behavior and tone. Concise bullets are behavioral guidance.
A system prompt can define the assistant's role. This instruction establishes the desired role.
A system prompt can establish guardrails. Refusing diagnosis requests is a safety boundary.

options.text: Set a maximum of 100 output tokens
options.rationale: A response-length cap is configured with max output tokens. It is not behavior or guardrail guidance in the system prompt.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant may follow its policy but still lack the requested length cap.
feedback.instructional: Put role, style, and guardrails in the system prompt; configure length with max output tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Style, role, and refusal rules are all appropriate system-prompt instructions.

exercises.question_text: To test prompts and capture working settings before coding, use the Foundry ___.

parts.text: To test prompts and capture working settings before coding, use the Foundry

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The selected tool would not provide the intended interactive testing workspace.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use the playground for prompt testing; use the catalog for discovery and APIs for code calls.

exercises.explanation: The Foundry playground is the portal interface for testing prompts and settings.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The request-rate limit would be stated unclearly.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with RPM, then state that it limits requests each minute.

exercises.correct_answer: RPM limits the number of requests handled each minute.
exercises.explanation: RPM refers to the number of requests handled per minute, not token traffic.

exercises.question_text: Before writing client code for a code helper, a developer needs to test prompts and save settings that work. Where should the developer start?

options.rationale: The playground lets a developer try prompts and capture working settings. It is designed for this pre-code testing task.
The catalog helps discover and compare models. It is not the interactive prompt-testing interface.
options.better_fit: Use this when the developer first needs to compare available models.

feedback.intrinsic: The developer may compare models without validating prompts.
feedback.instructional: Use the playground for prompt tests and settings capture.

options.rationale: The Responses API is for programmatic calls from code. The developer needs interactive testing before writing that code.
options.better_fit: Use this when implementing the client after testing is complete.

feedback.intrinsic: Implementation could start before the prompts are validated.
feedback.instructional: Test in the playground before moving settings into API code.

options.rationale: A lightweight chat client is an application to build. It is not the pre-code workspace for testing prompts.
options.better_fit: Use this when building a simple application interface.

feedback.intrinsic: Time could be spent building a client before its settings are known.
feedback.instructional: The playground is the efficient place to validate prompts first.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Start in the Foundry playground.

exercises.question_text: A virtual support agent gets rate-limit errors during busy periods. Which changes can help? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: High output-token settings can increase token use. Lowering them can reduce rate-limit pressure.
Too many concurrent requests can cause rate-limit errors. Reducing concurrency can help relieve pressure.
Temperature changes variation and repeatability. It is not a stated remedy for rate-limit pressure.
options.better_fit: Use this when changing response creativity or consistency.

options.better_fit: Use this when changing role, tone, or rules.

feedback.intrinsic: Responses may change while the workload still exceeds limits.
feedback.instructional: Throttling relates to processing limits, not instruction wording.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lowering output limits and concurrency can ease rate-limit pressure.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form a correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The directional relationship between temperature and variation would be unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Begin with higher temperature, then connect it to more creative variation.

exercises.correct_answer: Higher temperature generally favors more creative variation in responses.
exercises.explanation: Temperature balances variation and repeatability; moving it higher favors the variation side of that balance.

options.rationale: Temperature affects response repeatability. It is relevant when answers need to be consistent.
Instructions provide behavior guidance for the assistant. They help ensure the agent follows the intended response policy.

options.rationale: Deployment type determines where and how inference is processed. It does not directly set answer consistency.
options.better_fit: Use this when throughput and data-processing requirements drive the choice.

feedback.intrinsic: Processing could change while common answers remain inconsistent.
feedback.instructional: Deployment type handles processing; temperature affects repeatability.

Temperature changes variation and repeatability. It does not impose a firm length cap.

options.rationale: Deployment type determines where and how inference is processed. It does not set response length.
options.better_fit: Use this when selecting processing based on deployment requirements.

feedback.intrinsic: Processing may change while snippets remain too long.
feedback.instructional: Use deployment type for processing and max output tokens for length.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Max output tokens provides the requested cap.

exercises.question_text: What is a token?

options.text: A smallest unit of text or data
options.rationale: A token is a smallest unit of text or data a model processes. It can be a word, subword, character, or punctuation.
RPM counts requests per minute. Tokens are units within processed text or data.
options.better_fit: Use this idea when discussing request count per minute.

Max output tokens sets the response-length cap. A system prompt instead sets behavior-related guidance.

exercises.question_text: The Foundry playground is used only after all application code is written.

exercises.question_text: The prompt that establishes an assistant's behavior and role is the ___.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The prompt type would be mislabeled.

options.rationale: Deployment type is connected to throughput and data-processing requirements. It therefore best addresses the stated constraints.
A model version identifies a release. It does not address the deployment processing arrangement.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about token and request limits are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: TPM limits token traffic per minute
options.rationale: TPM is an allocation and rate limit for token traffic per minute. It measures token capacity over time.
RPM limits how many requests can be handled per minute. It counts requests rather than tokens.
Temperature controls response variation. RPM controls request count per minute.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The directional relationship between temperature and variation would be unclear.
